We propose that the sharp transitions in attention-based networks arise due to a specific chain of multi-layer operations necessary to achieve ICL, which is implemented by nested nonlinearities sequentially learned during training.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Tracing Facts or just Copies? A critical investigation of the Competitions of Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in LLMs mediate the competition between factual recall from parametric memory and counterfactual information provided in context? Do they perform selective counterfactual suppression or general copy suppression, and are they domain-specific?
papers.core_contribution: Attention heads that promote factual output in LLMs operate via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, and their behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models showing more specialization.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that attention heads mediate the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens via copy suppression, and their effects are domain-dependent, with implications for model interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads contribute to the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens, and modifying their strength affects the proportion of factual outputs.
The attention heads supporting factual tokens suppress copying in general, not just counterfactuals, as they also suppress factual tokens when facts are present in the prompt.
The effect of attention heads is sensitive to sentence structure and the presence of hints (factual token in the subject).
Attention heads exhibit domain specialization; their contribution varies by answer category (e.g., location, language, organization).
Larger models (Pythia-6.9B) show more specialized and category-sensitive patterns than smaller models (GPT-2).
papers.limitation: The experiments are limited to two models (GPT-2 and Pythia-6.9B) and do not cover more models or study attention modification of different heads on different domains in detail.
future_direction: Applying the methods to different models
Studying how each attention head interacts with different domains
Constructing new datasets on other domains (e.g., STEM) and applying similar techniques
papers.abstract: This paper presents a reproducibility study examining how Large Language Models (LLMs) manage competing factual and counterfactual information, focusing on the role of attention heads in this process. We attempt to reproduce and reconcile findings from three recent studies by Ortu et al., Yu, Merullo, and Pavlick and McDougall et al. that investigate the competition between model-learned facts and contradictory context information through Mechanistic Interpretability tools. Our study specifically examines the relationship between attention head strength and factual output ratios, evaluates competing hypotheses about attention heads' suppression mechanisms, and investigates the domain specificity of these attention patterns. Our findings suggest that attention heads promoting factual output do so via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, as strengthening them can also inhibit correct facts. Additionally, we show that attention head behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models exhibiting more specialized and category-sensitive patterns.

papers.title: Mechanism and Emergence of Stacked Attention Heads in Multi-Layer Transformers
papers.research_question: What tasks require transformers of a specific depth? Can large language models solve such tasks without fine-tuning? What mechanism do transformers use to solve the task? How does this mechanism emerge during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the retrieval problem, a task requiring a minimum number of transformer layers, and uncovers that transformers solve it using stacked attention heads (retrieval heads) which emerge gradually via an implicit curriculum.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces the retrieval problem, shows it requires a certain number of layers, and finds transformers solve it using a mechanism resembling an induction head that emerges gradually with the help of an implicit curriculum.
papers.key_findings:
The retrieval problem requires a minimum number of transformer layers that grows logarithmically with the number of retrieval steps.
Large language models can solve the retrieval problem without any specific fine-tuning.
Transformers solve the retrieval problem using stacked attention heads that resemble induction heads.
Retrieval heads emerge gradually during training, one head at a time, guided by an implicit curriculum.
The implicit curriculum is essential for successful learning of the retrieval problem.
papers.limitation:
The analysis of transformers trained on a minimal formulation of the retrieval problem might not generalize perfectly to large language models.
The paper does not provide a full explanation of the training dynamics of transformers on the retrieval problem.
future_direction: Further research is needed to fully understand the multi-layered circuits learned by large language models and the training dynamics that enable their learning.
papers.abstract: In this paper, I introduce the retrieval problem, a simple yet common reasoning task that can be solved only by transformers with a minimum number of layers, which grows logarithmically with the input size. I empirically show that large language models can solve the task under different prompting formulations without any fine-tuning. To understand how transformers solve the retrieval problem, I train several transformers on a minimal formulation. Successful learning occurs only under the presence of an implicit curriculum. I uncover the learned mechanisms by studying the attention maps in the trained transformers. I also study the training process, uncovering that attention heads always emerge in a specific sequence guided by the implicit curriculum.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Complexity Control Facilitates Reasoning-Based Compositional Generalization in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do complexity control strategies like initialization scale and weight decay influence transformers' ability to learn reasoning-based solutions for compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Complexity control strategies, such as small initialization scales and large weight decay, enable transformers to learn reasoning-based solutions for compositional tasks, leading to better out-of-distribution generalization.
papers.conclusion: Complexity control through initialization and weight decay is key to enabling transformers to learn compositional rules and generalize out-of-distribution.
papers.key_findings:
Models exhibit three phases based on initialization: poor generalization, good ID but poor OOD, and good ID and OOD generalization.
Complexity control (small init, large weight decay) promotes reasoning-based solutions with lower complexity bias.
Masking reveals that reasoning-based solutions use key token and anchor information differently.
Neuron condensation and structured embeddings are associated with reasoning phases.
Findings generalize to real-world tasks like image generation and NLP.
papers.abstract: Transformers have demonstrated impressive capabilities across various tasks, yet their performance on compositional problems remains a subject of debate. In this study, we investigate the internal mechanisms underlying Transformers' behavior in compositional tasks. We find that complexity control strategies significantly influence whether the model learns primitive-level rules that generalize out-of-distribution (reasoning-based solutions) or relies solely on memorized mappings (memory-based solutions). By applying masking strategies to the model's information circuits and employing multiple complexity metrics, we reveal distinct internal working mechanisms associated with different solution types. Further analysis reveals that reasoning-based solutions exhibit a lower complexity bias, which aligns with the well-studied neuron condensation phenomenon. This lower complexity bias is hypothesized to be the key factor enabling these solutions to learn reasoning rules. We validate these conclusions across multiple real-world datasets, including image generation and natural language processing tasks, confirming the broad applicability of our findings.

papers.title: Overlap in meaning is a stronger predictor of semantic activation in GPT-3 than in humans
papers.research_question: What are the similarities and differences in semantic activation patterns between GPT-3 and humans, particularly regarding the role of semantic similarity versus associative similarity?
papers.core_contribution: GPT-3's semantic activation patterns are broadly similar to humans, but semantic similarity is a stronger predictor of activation in GPT-3 than associative similarity, unlike in humans where associative similarity plays a larger role.
papers.conclusion: GPT-3's semantic network is organized more around word meaning than co-occurrence, suggesting differences from human semantic memory, but with similarities that can inform psycholinguistic research.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-3 shows higher semantic activation for first-associate word pairs compared to other-associate and unrelated pairs, similar to humans.
GPT-3's semantic activation is more strongly driven by semantic similarity (e.g., synonyms, antonyms) than by associative similarity (e.g., phrasal associates).
Humans show relatively stronger activation for associatively similar words, while GPT-3 shows stronger activation for semantically similar words.
The importance of semantic similarity in predicting activation increases with model complexity and recency.
Differences in measurement approaches (direct cosine similarity vs. indirect reaction times) may contribute to observed disparities.
papers.limitation: Semantic priming effects in humans measured via lexical decision tasks may be affected by processes like expectancy or semantic matching, introducing noise or bias not present in GPT-3's direct measurement.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models generate texts that are virtually indistinguishable from those written by humans and achieve near-human performance in comprehension and reasoning tests. Yet, their complexity makes it difficult to explain and predict their functioning. We examined a state-of-the-art language model (GPT-3) using lexical decision tasks widely used to study the structure of semantic memory in humans. The results of four analyses showed that GPT-3's patterns of semantic activation are broadly similar to those observed in humans, showing significantly higher semantic activation in related (e.g., "lime-lemon") word pairs than in other-related (e.g., "sour-lemon") or unrelated (e.g., "tourist-lemon") word pairs. However, there are also significant differences between GPT-3 and humans. GPT-3's semantic activation is better predicted by similarity in words' meaning (i.e., semantic similarity) rather than their co-occurrence in the language (i.e., associative similarity). This suggests that GPT-3's semantic network is organized around word meaning rather than their co-occurrence in text.

papers.title: Dissecting Persona-Driven Reasoning in Language Models via Activation Patching
papers.research_question: How does assigning a persona influence a language model's reasoning on an objective task, and what are the causal mechanisms within the model that give rise to persona-driven behavior and potential social bias?
papers.core_contribution: Early MLP layers encode persona-specific semantic information, which is then used by middle MHA layers to influence reasoning, and specific attention heads disproportionately attend to racial and color-based identities.
papers.conclusion: The work takes initial steps toward understanding the origins of persona-driven behavior in LLMs and demonstrates how activation patching can pinpoint components that encode and act upon persona-driven biases, offering a pathway for targeted bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Early MLP layers (layers 1-3) process semantic content related to persona, not just syntactic structure, and transform persona tokens into richer representations.
Middle MHA layers (layers 9-11) use the persona information from early MLPs to shape the model's output.
Specific attention heads (e.g., H25_9, H25_10, H26_11) disproportionately attend to tokens representing racial and color-based identities.
Patching activations from early MLP layers (especially at the identity token position) can reduce bias and restore model performance.
The effect of early MLP layers on output is indirect, mediated by later layers.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on Llama 3.2 1B, 3B, and Qwen 1.5B Instruct models, with head-level patching limited to Llama 1B due to computational constraints.
The MMLU dataset is not the only dataset meeting the selection criteria, but it was chosen for its objective, multiple-choice format.
The list of 16 personas is not exhaustive but serves as a practical starting point.
Attention pattern analysis requires manual inspection, which is slow and labor-intensive.
future_direction: Investigate why certain personas answer specific questions correctly while others do not.
Explore how output vector circuits in attention heads use earlier-layer representations to shape final predictions.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: On the Emergence of Position Bias in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do attention masks and positional encodings shape position bias in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a graph-theoretic framework for analyzing position bias in transformers, revealing that causal masking biases attention toward earlier positions and that relative positional encodings introduce a trade-off between decay effects and cumulative importance of early positions.
papers.conclusion: Our work provides a probabilistic and graph-theoretic framework for understanding position bias in transformers, revealing the inherent bias of causal masks toward earlier tokens and the nuanced interplay with relative positional encodings, offering a foundation for designing attention mechanisms with predictable positional properties.
papers.key_findings:
Causal masking inherently biases attention toward earlier positions in deep networks, as tokens in deeper layers attend to increasingly more contextualized representations of earlier tokens.
The interaction between causal masking and relative positional encodings (e.g., decay mask, RoPE) leads to a trade-off: while they introduce distance-based decay within individual layers, their aggregate effect across layers results in non-monotonic behavior, balancing local decay and cumulative importance of early positions.
Attention sinks emerge as center nodes in the graph defined by the attention mask, explaining why they appear at certain positions (e.g., first token for causal mask, prefix tokens for prefix mask).
The causal mask does not simulate positional encodings but instead introduces a bias toward earlier positions via iterative attention, capturing positional bias only when it aligns with this predisposition.
Residual connections can modulate the accumulation of positional effects across layers, making the relationship between depth and bias non-monotonic.
papers.limitation: The analysis does not extend to other transformer components such as residual connections, value projections, and MLPs, which may interact with attention in nontrivial ways.
future_direction: Leveraging insights to design bias-free transformers, mitigating positional biases to improve model robustness and generalization.
Informing the strategic exploitation of positional bias in specific applications, such as text summarization or recommendation systems.
Extending the analysis to other transformer components, such as residual connections, value projections, and MLPs.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have revealed various manifestations of position bias in transformer architectures, from the "lost-in-the-middle" phenomenon to attention sinks, yet a comprehensive theoretical understanding of how attention masks and positional encodings shape these biases remains elusive. This paper presents a graph-theoretic framework for analyzing position bias in multi-layer attention. Modeling attention masks as directed graphs, we quantify how tokens interact with contextual information based on their sequential positions. We uncover two key insights: First, causal masking inherently biases attention toward earlier positions, as tokens in deeper layers attend to increasingly more contextualized representations of earlier tokens. Second, we characterize the competing effects of the causal mask and relative positional encodings, such as the decay mask and rotary positional encoding (RoPE): while both mechanisms introduce distance-based decay within individual attention maps, their aggregate effect across multiple attention layers$\unicode{x2013}$coupled with the causal mask$\unicode{x2013}$leads to a trade-off between the long-term decay effects and the cumulative importance of early sequence positions. Through controlled numerical experiments, we not only validate our theoretical findings but also reproduce position biases observed in real-world LLMs. Our framework offers a principled foundation for understanding positional biases in transformers, shedding light on the complex interplay of attention mechanism components and guiding more informed architectural design.

papers.title: On the weak link between importance and prunability of attention heads
papers.research_question: Can we randomly prune attention heads, ignoring any notion of importance derived from interpretability studies, and what is the link between a head's interpreted importance and its prunability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds a weak link between the interpreted importance of attention heads and their prunability, showing that random pruning performs nearly as well as pruning based on importance, and that fine-tuning compensates for pruned heads uniformly across the network.
papers.conclusion: There is often no direct entailment between the importance of an attention head as characterized in interpretability studies and its low prunability when using random pruning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
A large fraction of attention heads can be randomly pruned with limited effect on accuracy (e.g., 75% in Transformer with <1 BLEU drop, 50% in BERT with <1% accuracy drop).
For Transformers, there is no advantage in pruning attention heads identified as important based on their location (e.g., layer or component).
For BERT, pruning top and bottom layers shows no significant difference, but pruning middle layers or consecutive layers leads to a larger drop in accuracy.
During fine-tuning, the compensation for pruned attention heads is roughly equally distributed across the un-pruned heads, with no spatial patterns in parameter changes.
papers.abstract: Given the success of Transformer-based models, two directions of study have emerged: interpreting role of individual attention heads and down-sizing the models for efficiency. Our work straddles these two streams: We analyse the importance of basing pruning strategies on the interpreted role of the attention heads. We evaluate this on Transformer and BERT models on multiple NLP tasks. Firstly, we find that a large fraction of the attention heads can be randomly pruned with limited effect on accuracy. Secondly, for Transformers, we find no advantage in pruning attention heads identified to be important based on existing studies that relate importance to the location of a head. On the BERT model too we find no preference for top or bottom layers, though the latter are reported to have higher importance. However, strategies that avoid pruning middle layers and consecutive layers perform better. Finally, during fine-tuning the compensation for pruned attention heads is roughly equally distributed across the un-pruned heads. Our results thus suggest that interpretation of attention heads does not strongly inform pruning.

papers.title: Copy Suppression: Comprehensively Understanding a Motif in Language Model Attention Heads
papers.research_question: What is the copy suppression motif in language model attention heads, and how does it explain the behavior of negative heads like L10H7 in GPT-2 Small?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces and comprehensively analyzes the copy suppression motif in language model attention heads, showing it explains 76.9% of L10H7's behavior in GPT-2 Small and plays a role in self-repair.
papers.conclusion: Copy suppression is a fundamental motif in language model attention heads that explains negative head behavior and contributes to self-repair, with implications for mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Copy suppression is a major role of negative attention heads like L10H7 in GPT-2 Small, explaining 76.9% of its behavior on OpenWebText.
The copy suppression mechanism involves three steps: naive copying by earlier components, attention to the previous instance, and suppression via writing against the unembedding.
Copy suppression improves model calibration by reducing overconfidence in incorrect copies.
Copy suppression is a form of self-repair, explaining 39% of self-repair in the IOI task after ablating name mover heads.
Copy suppression heads exist across model scales and architectures (e.g., Pythia-6B, Llama-2).
papers.limitation:
The idealized QK circuit analysis does not completely faithfully represent L10H7's real functioning.
The explanation does not account for when or how much copy suppression is activated in different contexts.
Using KL divergence as an ablation metric has limitations.
future_direction: Probe self-repair further.

papers.title: Attention as Binding: A Vector-Symbolic Perspective on Transformer Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can transformer attention be understood as a soft binding/unbinding operator in the framework of Vector Symbolic Architectures, and what does this perspective reveal about the logical reasoning capabilities and failures of transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops a unified perspective interpreting transformer self-attention and residual streams as implementing an approximate Vector Symbolic Architecture (VSA), providing an algebraic framework to explain reasoning capabilities and failure modes, and proposes a research agenda for VSA-inspired architectures.
papers.conclusion: Viewing attention as soft vector-symbolic computation offers a principled route toward more interpretable and logically reliable reasoning systems.
papers.key_findings:
Attention can be interpreted as a soft binding/unbinding operator where queries and keys define roles, values encode fillers, and attention weights perform soft unbinding.
Residual connections realize superposition of many bound structures, approximating VSA-style storage.
This VSA perspective explains characteristic transformer failure modes such as variable confusion and logical inconsistency.
The paper proposes architectural biases (e.g., explicit binding heads, hyperdimensional memory layers) and training objectives to promote VSA-like behavior for more robust reasoning.
The framework links transformer internals to chain-of-thought traces, program-based reasoning, and memory-augmented tool use.
future_direction: Designing VSA-inspired transformer layers with explicit binding/unbinding heads and hyperdimensional memory layers.
Developing training objectives and regularizers to promote role-filler separation and robust superposition.
Defining and measuring 'VSA-likeness' metrics and logical compositionality benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models display impressive reasoning-like behavior, yet remain brittle on tasks that require stable symbolic manipulation. This paper develops a unified perspective on these phenomena by interpreting self-attention and residual streams as implementing an approximate Vector Symbolic Architecture (VSA). In this view, queries and keys define role spaces, values encode fillers, attention weights perform soft unbinding, and residual connections realize superposition of many bound structures. We use this algebraic lens to relate transformer internals to chain-of-thought traces, program-based reasoning, and memory-augmented tool use, and to explain characteristic failure modes such as variable confusion and inconsistency across logically related prompts. Building on this perspective, we propose VSA-inspired architectural biases, including explicit binding/unbinding heads and hyperdimensional memory layers, and training objectives that promote role-filler separation and robust superposition. Finally, we outline metrics for measuring "VSA-likeness" and logical compositionality, and pose theoretical and architectural open problems. Overall, the paper argues that viewing attention as soft vector-symbolic computation offers a principled route toward more interpretable and logically reliable reasoning systems.

papers.title: Interpreting Key Mechanisms of Factual Recall in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models perform factual recall, specifically how do they extract arguments from context and apply implicit functions through MLPs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a detailed mechanistic interpretation of factual recall in transformers, introducing a method to decompose MLP outputs and identifying a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper outlines a pipeline for factual recall in transformers, proposes a novel analytic method for MLPs, and identifies a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism that can be mitigated to improve factual recall confidence.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific attention heads extract topic tokens and pass them to subsequent MLPs.
MLPs act as activations that amplify or erase individual attention head outputs in the residual stream.
Deep MLPs apply implicit functions by adding a task-aware component that redirects the residual stream towards the correct answer.
A universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer suppresses correct predictions, which can be mitigated using the proposed interpretation.
These mechanisms are consistent across models (GPT-2, OPT, Llama-2), tasks (country-capital, product-developer), and few-shot settings.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not explore how the model constructs task semantics within its shallow layers.
The origins of the identified mechanisms (e.g., why MLPs redirect the residual stream) need further research.
The proposed analysis method for decomposing MLP outputs requires preliminary human reasoning and is not fully automated.
future_direction: Exploring how task semantics are constructed in shallow layers through collaborative circuit paths.
Investigating the origins of the mechanisms, such as why MLP outputs are structured as y-x.
Developing more automated interpretation techniques for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we delve into several mechanisms employed by Transformer-based language models (LLMs) for factual recall tasks. We outline a pipeline consisting of three major steps: (1) Given a prompt ``The capital of France is,'' task-specific attention heads extract the topic token, such as ``France,'' from the context and pass it to subsequent MLPs. (2) As attention heads' outputs are aggregated with equal weight and added to the residual stream, the subsequent MLP acts as an ``activation,'' which either erases or amplifies the information originating from individual heads. As a result, the topic token ``France'' stands out in the residual stream. (3) A deep MLP takes ``France'' and generates a component that redirects the residual stream towards the direction of the correct answer, i.e., ``Paris.'' This procedure is akin to applying an implicit function such as ``get\_capital($X$),'' and the argument $X$ is the topic token information passed by attention heads. To achieve the above quantitative and qualitative analysis for MLPs, we proposed a novel analytic method aimed at decomposing the outputs of the MLP into components understandable by humans. Additionally, we observed a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer of models, which suppresses correct predictions. We mitigate this suppression by leveraging our interpretation to improve factual recall confidence. The above interpretations are evaluated across diverse tasks spanning various domains of factual knowledge, using various language models from the GPT-2 families, 1.3B OPT, up to 7B Llama-2, and in both zero- and few-shot setups.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How does arithmetic ability work in large language models, and why do only a few attention heads significantly impact arithmetic performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, constructs an internal logic chain with four stages, and applies CNA to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias editing.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic operations, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons' coefficient scores, and applies the method for model pruning and bias editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability resides in a limited number of attention heads, with each head specializing in distinct operations.
CNA identifies an internal logic chain from input to prediction with four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
The method can be used for model pruning on arithmetic tasks, achieving good performance with only 5% of deep FFN neurons.
The method can identify and edit FFN neurons to reduce gender bias in model outputs.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which lacks complete theoretical foundation.
Lack of standardization across attribution methods; gradient-based and SHAP methods are computationally expensive.
Potential risk that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to maliciously change model outputs.
future_direction: Further investigation of why multiplication heads do not significantly impact accuracy.
Exploration of the method on different gender bias datasets.
Investigating how to distinguish whether a model has been edited maliciously.
papers.abstract: We find arithmetic ability resides within a limited number of attention heads, with each head specializing in distinct operations. To delve into the reason, we introduce the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method, which identifies an internal logic chain consisting of four distinct stages from input to prediction: feature enhancing with shallow FFN neurons, feature transferring by shallow attention layers, feature predicting by arithmetic heads, and prediction enhancing among deep FFN neurons. Moreover, we identify the human-interpretable FFN neurons within both feature-enhancing and feature-predicting stages. These findings lead us to investigate the mechanism of LoRA, revealing that it enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of FFN neurons related to predictions. Finally, we apply our method in model pruning for arithmetic tasks and model editing for reducing gender bias. Code is on https://github.com/zepingyu0512/arithmetic-mechanism.

papers.title: Start Making Sense(s): A Developmental Probe of Attention Specialization Using Lexical Ambiguity
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in Transformer language models develop specialized attention patterns for word sense disambiguation, and how robust are these heads to stimulus perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a developmental pipeline to probe attention specialization in Transformer LMs, using lexical ambiguity to identify and causally validate attention heads involved in word sense disambiguation, finding that larger models have more robust disambiguation heads.
papers.conclusion: Disambiguation benefits from a constellation of mechanisms, some of which are highly sensitive to cue position and part-of-speech (especially in smaller models), while larger models contain more robust disambiguation heads, highlighting the value of a developmental perspective in probing LM mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Disambiguation performance improves with model size but with diminishing returns, with 410M achieving 92% of the performance of 12B despite having 3% as many parameters.
Inflection points in disambiguation performance occur early in pre-training (e.g., at steps 1000 and 2000).
In Pythia-14M, specific attention heads (e.g., (3,1) and (3,2)) show attention patterns that covary with disambiguation performance.
In Pythia-410M, multiple heads across layers show robust disambiguation behavior, generalizing across stimulus perturbations like positional and part-of-speech changes.
Ablating identified heads causally impairs disambiguation performance, especially in Pythia-14M, confirming their functional role.
papers.abstract: Despite an in-principle understanding of self-attention matrix operations in Transformer language models (LMs), it remains unclear precisely how these operations map onto interpretable computations or functions--and how or when individual attention heads develop specialized attention patterns. Here, we present a pipeline to systematically probe attention mechanisms, and we illustrate its value by leveraging lexical ambiguity--where a single word has multiple meanings--to isolate attention mechanisms that contribute to word sense disambiguation. We take a "developmental" approach: first, using publicly available Pythia LM checkpoints, we identify inflection points in disambiguation performance for each LM in the suite; in 14M and 410M, we identify heads whose attention to disambiguating words covaries with overall disambiguation performance across development. We then stress-test the robustness of these heads to stimulus perturbations: in 14M, we find limited robustness, but in 410M, we identify multiple heads with surprisingly generalizable behavior. Then, in a causal analysis, we find that ablating the target heads demonstrably impairs disambiguation performance, particularly in 14M. We additionally reproduce developmental analyses of 14M across all of its random seeds. Together, these results suggest: that disambiguation benefits from a constellation of mechanisms, some of which (especially in 14M) are highly sensitive to the position and part-of-speech of the disambiguating cue; and that larger models (410M) may contain heads with more robust disambiguation behavior. They also join a growing body of work that highlights the value of adopting a developmental perspective when probing LM mechanisms.

papers.title: Allocation of Parameters in Transformers
papers.research_question: How should the model parameters – mainly attention heads and head dimensions – be allocated across Transformer layers to balance expressivity and efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides theoretical analysis and experimental validation to derive principled strategies for allocating attention heads and head dimensions across Transformer layers, improving model efficiency.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a theoretical foundation for parameter allocation in Transformers and offers practical guidelines for designing efficient architectures.
papers.key_findings:
There is a trade-off between the number of attention heads and head dimensions for information extraction in early layers, given a fixed parameter budget.
Softmax activations exhibit a saturation pattern where increasing head dimensions yields diminishing returns, especially for long sequences, enabling parameter reduction in later layers.
Principled parameter allocation strategies can be formulated based on the approximation error estimate and the softmax saturation behavior.
Numerical experiments on tasks like 4-gram modeling and head compression validate the theoretical trade-offs and saturation patterns.
The proposed allocation strategies can guide the design of more parameter-efficient Transformer architectures.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on single-layer and shallow Transformers; extending it to deep architectures and more complex tasks is an important future direction.
The proposed strategies require validation in large-scale pretraining and transfer learning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deep Transformer architectures and more complex tasks.
Exploring alternative attention mechanisms and their interactions with feed-forward modules and optimization.
Validating the allocation strategies in large-scale pretraining and transfer learning to reduce computation and memory costs.
papers.abstract: Transformers have achieved remarkable successes across a wide range of applications, yet the theoretical foundation of their model efficiency remains underexplored. In this work, we investigate how the model parameters -- mainly attention heads and head dimensions -- should be allocated across layers to balance expressivity and efficiency. We first provide mathematical analysis on the role of early layers in information extraction from an approximation perspective, with a theoretical characterization on the trade-off between the number of heads and head dimension under a fixed parameter budget. In addition, we uncover and prove the \emph{saturation} behavior of softmax activations: Continuously increasing head dimensions can lead to diminishing returns in learning errors, particularly for long sequences. Supported by both theory and experiments, this saturation pattern suggests that later layers can operate more efficiently with reduced parameters. Combining these insights, we propose principled strategies for allocating attention heads and dimensions across Transformers' layers, shedding light on theoretically-grounded model efficiency of Transformer-based architectures.

papers.title: Tracing Stereotypes in Pre-trained Transformers: From Biased Neurons to Fairer Models
papers.research_question: To what extent can we identify biased neurons in pre-trained transformers? Does suppressing biased neurons reduce the likelihood that models generate stereotypical outputs? What is the impact of suppressing biased neurons on models' performance in SE tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that biased knowledge in transformers is localized within small subsets of neurons (biased neurons), and that suppressing these neurons substantially reduces bias with minimal performance loss on downstream software engineering tasks.
papers.conclusion: Bias in transformers can be traced and mitigated at the neuron level, offering an interpretable and fine-grained approach to fairness in software engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Biased knowledge is encoded in sparse, localized subsets of neurons (1-3 neurons per relation) rather than being diffusely distributed.
Suppressing biased neurons (zeroing their activations) causally reduces the model's confidence in generating stereotypical outputs, as measured by increased perplexity on bias-activating prompts.
Suppressing biased neurons has a limited and task-dependent impact on downstream performance in non-code SE tasks, with variations in accuracy and F1 typically within a few percentage points.
Fine-tuned BERT models exhibit greater robustness to neuron suppression than raw pre-trained models, often maintaining or slightly improving performance on SE tasks.
The neuron-level tracing and suppression approach offers an interpretable and fine-grained method for bias mitigation without requiring model retraining.
papers.limitation:
The construction of the biased relations dataset using GPT-4o may introduce inaccuracies, though mitigated by manual validation.
Experiments are limited to BERT-based models, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures (e.g., GPT, T5, RoBERTa).
The five non-code SE tasks evaluated may not cover the entire SE spectrum, though they represent realistic, fairness-relevant scenarios.
The sample (nine bias categories and four model variants) may limit large-scale generalization.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to generative and instruction-tuned models.
Explore causal links between biased and factual neurons.
Automate the tracing and suppression process.
Study how neuron-level fairness interventions interact with broader SE practices.
papers.abstract: The advent of transformer-based language models has reshaped how AI systems process and generate text. In software engineering (SE), these models now support diverse activities, accelerating automation and decision-making. Yet, evidence shows that these models can reproduce or amplify social biases, raising fairness concerns. Recent work on neuron editing has shown that internal activations in pre-trained transformers can be traced and modified to alter model behavior. Building on the concept of knowledge neurons, neurons that encode factual information, we hypothesize the existence of biased neurons that capture stereotypical associations within pre-trained transformers. To test this hypothesis, we build a dataset of biased relations, i.e., triplets encoding stereotypes across nine bias types, and adapt neuron attribution strategies to trace and suppress biased neurons in BERT models. We then assess the impact of suppression on SE tasks. Our findings show that biased knowledge is localized within small neuron subsets, and suppressing them substantially reduces bias with minimal performance loss. This demonstrates that bias in transformers can be traced and mitigated at the neuron level, offering an interpretable approach to fairness in SE.

papers.title: Transformers Are Born Biased: Structural Inductive Biases at Random Initialization and Their Practical Consequences
papers.research_question: Do randomly initialized transformers exhibit systematic structural biases, and what are their mechanisms and practical consequences?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers exhibit strong structural biases at random initialization due to representation contraction driven by MLP and attention, which persist through training and enable seed-specific fingerprinting (SeedPrint) and explain the attention-sink phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are not blank slates; they possess inherent structural biases at initialization that persist through training, with implications for model fingerprinting and architecture design.
papers.key_findings:
Randomly initialized transformers show extreme token preferences, with certain tokens predicted orders of magnitude more often than others.
This preference arises from inter-sequence representation contraction, where last-token representations from different sequences become highly similar.
The contraction is primarily driven by asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP layers, and amplified by self-attention through intra-sequence aggregation.
These initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable model identity that can be used for fingerprinting (SeedPrint).
The attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction leads to a positional discrepancy that causally explains the attention-sink phenomenon in trained LLMs.
future_direction: Design architectures that are more neutral or explicitly incorporate desired inductive biases.
Treat initialization choices as hyperparameters tuned for final model behavior, not just optimization stability.
Extend the fingerprinting method to more challenging scenarios, such as detecting obfuscated or distilled models.
papers.abstract: Transformers underpin modern large language models (LLMs) and are commonly assumed to be behaviorally unstructured at random initialization, with all meaningful preferences emerging only through large-scale training. We challenge this assumption by showing that randomly initialized transformers already exhibit strong and systematic structural biases. In particular, untrained models display extreme token preferences: across random input sequences, certain tokens are predicted with probabilities orders of magnitude larger. We provide a mechanistic explanation for this phenomenon by dissecting the transformer architecture at initialization. We show that extreme token preference arises from a contraction of token representations along a random seed-dependent direction. This contraction is driven by two interacting forces: (i) asymmetric nonlinear activations in MLP sublayers induce global (inter-sequence) representation concentration, and (ii) self-attention further amplifies this effect through local (intra-sequence) aggregation. Together, these mechanisms align hidden representations along a direction determined solely by the random initialization, producing highly non-uniform next-token predictions. Beyond mechanistic insight, we demonstrate that these initialization-induced biases persist throughout training, forming a stable and intrinsic model identity. Leveraging this property, we introduce SeedPrint, a fingerprinting method that can reliably distinguish models that differ only in their random initialization, even after extensive training and under substantial distribution shift. Finally, we identify a fundamental positional discrepancy inherent to the attention mechanism's intra-sequence contraction that is causally linked to the attention-sink phenomenon. This discovery provides a principled explanation for the emergence of sinks and offers a pathway for their control.

papers.title: Beyond the Black Box: Interpretability of LLMs in Finance
papers.research_question: How can mechanistic interpretability techniques be applied to understand and control the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) in financial applications to improve transparency and reliability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates the application of mechanistic interpretability techniques—Logit Lens, Attribution Patching, and Sparse Autoencoders—to financial use cases, showing how they can be used to understand, debug, and steer model behavior for tasks like sentiment analysis, bias detection, and hallucination reduction.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability offers a promising path to dissect and guide AI-driven financial decisions with greater transparency and control, though challenges in scalability, generalization, and mapping abstract features to human-understandable concepts remain.
papers.key_findings:
Logit Lens analysis reveals how token prediction probabilities evolve across transformer layers in response to financial prompts, showing refinement of predictions in deeper layers.
Attribution Patching identifies specific attention heads in layers 8 and 10 of GPT-2 as causally significant for correct financial predictions.
Sparse Autoencoders can extract interpretable, monosemantic features from model activations relevant to financial concepts like credit risk.
Feature steering via Sparse Autoencoders can modify model outputs, such as improving sentiment classification accuracy for credit risk analysis without fine-tuning.
A feature-activation-thresholded Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach can reduce hallucinations in financial question-answering by ensuring external factual data is incorporated when internal feature activations are low.
papers.limitation:
Scalability is a major concern, as manual circuit analysis becomes infeasible for very large models, and automated interpretability tools are still in early development.
Many techniques fail to generalize effectively to real-world financial applications, as models often rely on abstract representations not directly mappable to human-understandable financial concepts.
The evolving nature of financial markets and regulations means models trained on historical data may struggle to adapt, requiring dynamic interpretability pipelines.
Identifying a particular neuron or attention head does not always clarify the exact influence of features such as credit score or volatility on the final decision.
future_direction: Integrating mechanistic interpretability with feature-level attributions to ensure AI decisions are explainable in terms of real-world financial indicators.
Developing a hybrid approach that integrates traditional statistical modeling techniques using financial time series data with unstructured data processed by LLMs.
Building fully integrated interpretability tooling that combines techniques from various research efforts to streamline analysis workflows for financial professionals.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities across a spectrum of tasks in financial services, including report generation, chatbots, sentiment analysis, regulatory compliance, investment advisory, financial knowledge retrieval, and summarization. However, their intrinsic complexity and lack of transparency pose significant challenges, especially in the highly regulated financial sector, where interpretability, fairness, and accountability are critical. As far as we are aware, this paper presents the first application in the finance domain of understanding and utilizing the inner workings of LLMs through mechanistic interpretability, addressing the pressing need for transparency and control in AI systems. Mechanistic interpretability is the most intuitive and transparent way to understand LLM behavior by reverse-engineering their internal workings. By dissecting the activations and circuits within these models, it provides insights into how specific features or components influence predictions - making it possible not only to observe but also to modify model behavior. In this paper, we explore the theoretical aspects of mechanistic interpretability and demonstrate its practical relevance through a range of financial use cases and experiments, including applications in trading strategies, sentiment analysis, bias, and hallucination detection. While not yet widely adopted, mechanistic interpretability is expected to become increasingly vital as adoption of LLMs increases. Advanced interpretability tools can ensure AI systems remain ethical, transparent, and aligned with evolving financial regulations. In this paper, we have put special emphasis on how these techniques can help unlock interpretability requirements for regulatory and compliance purposes - addressing both current needs and anticipating future expectations from financial regulators globally.

papers.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
papers.research_question: How are factual associations stored and recalled in autoregressive transformer language models, and can they be directly edited?
papers.core_contribution: Factual associations in GPT are stored in mid-layer feed-forward modules and can be directly edited using a rank-one update method (ROME), which achieves strong generalization and specificity.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations in autoregressive transformers are stored in mid-layer MLP modules and can be directly edited via localized weight updates, with ROME providing an effective method for such edits.
papers.key_findings:
Causal tracing reveals that mid-layer MLP modules at the last subject token are decisive for factual predictions.
The Rank-One Model Editing (ROME) method can effectively edit factual associations by updating a single MLP layer with a rank-one weight update.
ROME achieves strong generalization and specificity on counterfactual edits, outperforming previous fine-tuning and hypernetwork-based methods.
The early site (mid-layer MLP) and late site (late-layer attention) play different roles: MLP stores the association, and attention copies it to the output.
The paper introduces a new dataset, COUNTERFACT, for evaluating counterfactual model edits.
papers.limitation: Human evaluation reveals a reduction in fluency of generated text under ROME, which the automatic entropy measure does not capture.
papers.abstract: We analyze the storage and recall of factual associations in autoregressive transformer language models, finding evidence that these associations correspond to localized, directly-editable computations. We first develop a causal intervention for identifying neuron activations that are decisive in a model's factual predictions. This reveals a distinct set of steps in middle-layer feed-forward modules that mediate factual predictions while processing subject tokens. To test our hypothesis that these computations correspond to factual association recall, we modify feed-forward weights to update specific factual associations using Rank-One Model Editing (ROME). We find that ROME is effective on a standard zero-shot relation extraction (zsRE) model-editing task, comparable to existing methods. To perform a more sensitive evaluation, we also evaluate ROME on a new dataset of counterfactual assertions, on which it simultaneously maintains both specificity and generalization, whereas other methods sacrifice one or another. Our results confirm an important role for mid-layer feed-forward modules in storing factual associations and suggest that direct manipulation of computational mechanisms may be a feasible approach for model editing. The code, dataset, visualizations, and an interactive demo notebook are available at https://rome.baulab.info/

papers.title: Analyzing Multi-Head Self-Attention: Specialized Heads Do the Heavy\n Lifting, the Rest Can Be Pruned
papers.research_question: What is the contribution of individual attention heads to translation performance? Do they play consistent and interpretable roles? Can the number of heads be significantly reduced without serious performance loss?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that only a subset of attention heads are important for translation, with interpretable functions, and introduces a pruning method that can remove the majority of heads without significant performance loss.
papers.conclusion: Specialized attention heads are most important for translation and can be identified, while many heads are redundant and can be pruned without serious performance loss.
papers.key_findings:
Only a small subset of attention heads are important for translation.
Important heads have specialized and interpretable functions, such as attending to adjacent tokens, specific syntactic relations, and rare words.
The proposed pruning method can remove the vast majority of heads (e.g., 38 out of 48 encoder heads) with only a small drop in BLEU (0.15).
Encoder self-attention heads are pruned first, while decoder-encoder attention heads are the most important.
Lower decoder layers retain self-attention heads for language modeling, while higher decoder layers retain decoder-encoder attention heads for conditioning on the source sentence.
papers.limitation: The impact of target language morphology on the accuracy of syntactic attention heads is not fully understood.
future_direction: Investigate how the pruning method compares to alternative methods of model compression in neural machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Multi-head self-attention is a key component of the Transformer, a
state-of-the-art architecture for neural machine translation. In this work we
evaluate the contribution made by individual attention heads in the encoder to
the overall performance of the model and analyze the roles played by them. We
find that the most important and confident heads play consistent and often
linguistically-interpretable roles. When pruning heads using a method based on
stochastic gates and a differentiable relaxation of the L0 penalty, we observe
that specialized heads are last to be pruned. Our novel pruning method removes
the vast majority of heads without seriously affecting performance. For
example, on the English-Russian WMT dataset, pruning 38 out of 48 encoder heads
results in a drop of only 0.15 BLEU.

papers.title: Losing Heads in the Lottery: Pruning Transformer Attention in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Can the lottery ticket hypothesis be applied to prune entire attention heads in transformers during early training to achieve faster inference with minimal impact on translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that the lottery ticket hypothesis can be applied to prune entire attention heads in transformers during early training, achieving significant inference speed-ups (up to 1.5x) with minimal loss in translation quality (e.g., -0.1 BLEU at 72% sparsity).
papers.conclusion: Block-wise pruning of attention heads via the lottery ticket hypothesis is effective, allowing removal of 50-72% of heads with minimal quality loss and significant speed-ups, and is complementary to other efficiency methods.
papers.key_findings:
The lottery ticket hypothesis can be applied to prune whole blocks of parameters (attention heads) instead of individual weights.
Most attention heads can be removed early in training without significant quality loss, with up to 72% sparsity causing only -0.1 BLEU change.
The lottery ticket approach achieves better results than training a model from scratch with the same pruned structure.
Pruned models show patterns in head distribution: context attention becomes more important in later layers, and decoder self-attention is only needed in the first layer.
Pruning attention heads leads to faster inference, with 1.5x speed-up for transformer-big and 10-15% speed-up for student models.
papers.limitation: The pruning procedure requires longer training time compared to the baseline.
future_direction: Prune other parts of the network (beyond attention heads) using block-wise pruning.
Improve the heuristic algorithm for selecting heads to prune.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is the crucial component of the transformer architecture. Recent research shows that most attention heads are not confident in their decisions and can be pruned after training. However, removing them before training a model results in lower quality. In this paper, we apply the lottery ticket hypothesis to prune heads in the early stages of training, instead of doing so on a fully converged model. Our experiments on machine translation show that it is possible to remove up to three-quarters of all attention heads from a transformer-big model with an average -0.1 change in BLEU for TurkishEnglish. The pruned model is 1.5 times as fast at inference, albeit at the cost of longer training. The method is complementary to other approaches, such as teacher-student, with our EnglishGerman student losing 0.2 BLEU at 75% encoder attention sparsity.

papers.title: Measuring the Mixing of Contextual Information in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How is contextual information mixed across the Transformer architecture, and how can this mixing be measured to provide faithful explanations for model predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes ALTI, an interpretability method that measures token-to-token interactions within each Transformer layer and aggregates them to provide input attribution scores, demonstrating more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: ALTI is a powerful interpretability method that quantifies the mixing of information in the Transformer, providing faithful input attributions and opening new possibilities for studying contextual information aggregation.
papers.key_findings:
ALTI outperforms gradient-based and other attribution methods in faithfulness metrics (comprehensiveness and sufficiency) across multiple models and datasets.
ALTI provides more robust interpretations across models with identical architecture but different random initializations, as measured by Jaccard similarity and Spearman correlation.
Using ℓ1 norm for measuring token contributions in ALTI is beneficial due to the anisotropic nature of Transformer representations and the presence of outlier dimensions.
The proposed layer-wise contribution measurement (based on distance to the output) significantly improves upon a previous norm-based approach.
Including the second layer normalization (from the feed-forward module) in the analysis has negligible impact on the faithfulness of the interpretations.
papers.limitation:
ALTI does not consider the classifier on top of the Transformer and therefore does not provide explanations for each of the output classes, unlike gradient-based methods.
Faithfulness is evaluated only via sufficiency and comprehensiveness metrics.
papers.abstract: The Transformer architecture aggregates input information through the self-attention mechanism, but there is no clear understanding of how this information is mixed across the entire model. Additionally, recent works have demonstrated that attention weights alone are not enough to describe the flow of information. In this paper, we consider the whole attention block --multi-head attention, residual connection, and layer normalization-- and define a metric to measure token-to-token interactions within each layer. Then, we aggregate layer-wise interpretations to provide input attribution scores for model predictions. Experimentally, we show that our method, ALTI (Aggregation of Layer-wise Token-to-token Interactions), provides more faithful explanations and increased robustness than gradient-based methods.

papers.title: Semantic Layer Reconstruction in Large Language Models Using Multi-Level Transformer Feedback Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How can semantic coherence in large language models be improved through recursive feedback mechanisms between transformer layers to address semantic drift and alignment inefficiencies?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Semantic Layer Reconstruction (SLR), a framework with multi-level feedback mechanisms to improve semantic alignment and coherence in transformer-based language models by recursively refining token embeddings across layers.
papers.conclusion: SLR successfully enhances semantic coherence in LLMs through recursive feedback, improving performance on various linguistic tasks and providing a scalable solution for layer interaction optimization.
papers.key_findings:
SLR reduces perplexity and improves BLEU scores and semantic similarity indices compared to baseline models.
Middle transformer layers contribute most to semantic alignment, as shown in layer-wise ablation analysis.
The feedback mechanism leads to more balanced attention weight distributions across tokens.
SLR enhances performance on long-range dependency tasks such as pronoun resolution and coreference tracking.
The model demonstrates resilience to moderate noise but performance declines with high noise levels.
papers.limitation:
Performance plateaus with excessively long input sequences due to diminishing returns in feedback mechanism.
Computational overhead from recursive feedback, though minimized, may impact deployment in resource-constrained environments.
future_direction: Developing adaptive feedback mechanisms that adjust based on input complexity and task-specific requirements.
Extending the SLR framework to multimodal contexts with visual or auditory inputs.
Incorporating domain-specific embeddings for low-resource languages or specialized domains.
papers.abstract: Semantic Layer Reconstruction introduces a transformative mechanism for refining the interactions between transformer layers, leveraging recursive feedback to enhance semantic coherence across linguistic tasks. The framework incorporates a multi-level feedback mechanism that recalibrates token embeddings through bidirectional propagation of semantic cues, addressing challenges such as semantic drift and alignment inefficiencies. By dynamically integrating higher-layer abstractions into earlier computational processes, the approach fosters a more coherent synthesis of token-level and contextual representations. Experimental evaluations reveal significant improvements in perplexity, BLEU scores, and semantic similarity indices, highlighting the framework's ability to address complex linguistic phenomena. Layer-wise analyses underscore the critical contributions of middle layers in achieving optimal semantic alignment, while attention-weight distributions demonstrate a more balanced contextual focus. The recursive feedback mechanism also proved instrumental in capturing long-range dependencies, showcasing its utility in tasks requiring deep contextual understanding. Comparative configurations further validated the adaptability of the mechanism, with dynamic recursive intervals outperforming static approaches across all metrics. Noise-resilience experiments highlighted the model's robustness, while visualizations of semantic drift reduction provided compelling evidence of improved coherence. The integration of the mechanism into existing transformer architectures maintained computational efficiency through optimizations such as sparse attention and modularity. The study bridges theoretical innovations with empirical validation, offering a scalable and adaptable solution for advancing the semantic capabilities of transformer-based architectures. The findings provide a foundation for redefining the paradigms of contextual representation and layer-wise interaction in contemporary language modeling.

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
