papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable performance, the lack of transparency in their inference logic raises concerns about their trustworthiness. To gain a better understanding of LLMs, we conduct a detailed analysis of the operations of attention heads and aim to better understand the in-context learning of LLMs. Specifically, we investigate whether attention heads encode two types of relationships between tokens present in natural languages: the syntactic dependency parsed from sentences and the relation within knowledge graphs. We find that certain attention heads exhibit a pattern where, when attending to head tokens, they recall tail tokens and increase the output logits of those tail tokens. More crucially, the formulation of such semantic induction heads has a close correlation with the emergence of the in-context learning ability of language models. The study of semantic attention heads advances our understanding of the intricate operations of attention heads in transformers, and further provides new insights into the in-context learning of LLMs.

papers.title: Traveling Words: A Geometric Interpretation of Transformers
papers.research_question: How can the internal mechanisms of transformers be understood from a geometric perspective, specifically the role of layer normalization and attention?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a geometric interpretation of transformers, showing how layer normalization projects features onto a hyper-sphere and how attention and feed-forward modules operate as geometric transformations on this sphere.
papers.conclusion: The geometric interpretation provides an intuitive understanding of transformers as processes that model the trajectory of word particles along the surface of a hyper-sphere, connecting and clarifying existing mechanistic insights.
papers.key_findings:
Layer normalization constrains d-dimensional input features to the surface of a (d-1) dimensional hyper-sphere.
Early attention heads show clear query-key patterns (e.g., repetition, precedence), while deeper layers exhibit more complex, subject-specific patterns.
The WV O matrix functions as a key-value store, and its singular value decomposition reveals interpretable, subject-specific singular vectors in deeper layers.
The geometric perspective unifies existing concepts like iterative refinement and contextual embeddings.
The word embedding matrix, when combined with layer normalization scale and bias, aligns common tokens with high-probability regions on the hyper-sphere.
papers.abstract: Transformers have significantly advanced the field of natural language processing, but comprehending their internal mechanisms remains a challenge. In this paper, we introduce a novel geometric perspective that elucidates the inner mechanisms of transformer operations. Our primary contribution is illustrating how layer normalization confines the latent features to a hyper-sphere, subsequently enabling attention to mold the semantic representation of words on this surface. This geometric viewpoint seamlessly connects established properties such as iterative refinement and contextual embeddings. We validate our insights by probing a pre-trained 124M parameter GPT-2 model. Our findings reveal clear query-key attention patterns in early layers and build upon prior observations regarding the subject-specific nature of attention heads at deeper layers. Harnessing these geometric insights, we present an intuitive understanding of transformers, depicting them as processes that model the trajectory of word particles along the hyper-sphere.

papers.title: Deconstructing Attention: Investigating Design Principles for Effective Language Modeling
papers.research_question: Which design principles of dot-product attention are essential for effective language modeling, and can some be relaxed in hybrid architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Token mixing is indispensable for language modeling, while the mathematical form and sequence dependency can be relaxed, especially in hybrid architectures where standard attention layers stabilize simpler variants.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that token mixing is essential, but other attention principles can be simplified, especially when standard attention layers are interleaved, leading to robust performance.
papers.key_findings:
Token mixing is crucial; without it, models perform near-random on NLU tasks.
The standard mathematical form is important in uniform configurations but can be relaxed in hybrid ones.
Sequence-dependency enhances generalization ability.
Current QK derivation is not as essential as expected.
Layer collaboration allows poor-performing variants to contribute in hybrid architectures.
papers.limitation: Experiments are limited to models up to 500M parameters, 15B tokens pretraining, and monolingual tokenizer.
future_direction: Experimenting with larger models and different model families.
papers.abstract: The success of Transformer language models is widely credited to their dot-product attention mechanism, which interweaves a set of key design principles: mixing information across positions (enabling multi-token interactions), sequence-dependent activations (where attention weights adapt to each input), a specific mathematical form (dot-product similarities plus softmax weighting), and coupling of queries and keys to evolving hidden states (grounding attention in the current layer). However, the necessity of each of these principles remains largely untested. In this work, we systematically deconstruct attention by designing controlled variants that selectively relax these principles, applied both uniformly across all layers and in hybrid architectures where only some layers retain standard attention. Our empirical analysis reveals that mechanisms for mixing tokens are indispensable, as their absence collapses models to near-random behavior, while the exact mathematical form and sequence dependency can be substantially relaxed, especially when preserved in just a subset of layers. Surprisingly, even variants that fail in isolation can achieve robust performance when interleaved with standard attention, highlighting a cooperative effect. These findings deepen our understanding of what truly underpins attention's effectiveness and open new avenues for simplifying language models without sacrificing performance.

papers.title: Beyond Semantics: How Temporal Biases Shape Retrieval in Transformer and State-Space Models
papers.research_question: How do temporal biases shape information retrieval in transformer and state-space models during in-context learning, and how effectively can these models differentiate and retrieve temporally separated events?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that both transformer and state-space models exhibit strong temporal biases (primacy and recency effects) in retrieving information, and in transformers, these biases are mechanistically linked to the function of induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Temporal biases are fundamental to in-context learning in both transformer and state-space architectures, shaping information retrieval in ways analogous to human episodic memory, with induction heads playing a key mechanistic role in transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Both transformer and state-space models show a tendency for serial recall, predicting the token immediately following a repeated instance ('+1' token).
The strength of serial recall is modulated by the token's temporal position, showing strong primacy and recency effects, with model-specific biases (e.g., Mistral shows recency, Falcon-Mamba shows primacy).
Ablating induction heads in transformers significantly impairs both serial recall and the ability to selectively retrieve correct episodes in the presence of interference, confirming their causal role.
Despite architectural differences, state-space models exhibit comparable temporal biases to transformers, suggesting these biases arise from fundamental properties of sequential data processing.
Episodic retrieval is less reliable for memories embedded in the middle of a prompt, demonstrating a 'lost in the middle' effect even when semantic content is neutralized.
papers.limitation: The study primarily uses token-random prompts rather than natural text and analyzes next-token probabilities, representing a simplified information environment that isolates temporal effects from semantic confounds.
future_direction: Future work can explore the more complex interplay between 'when' something was said and 'what' was said in rich, semantic contexts.
papers.abstract: In-context learning is governed by both temporal and semantic relationships, shaping how Large Language Models (LLMs) retrieve contextual information. Analogous to human episodic memory, where the retrieval of specific events is enabled by separating events that happened at different times, this work probes the ability of various pretrained LLMs, including transformer and state-space models, to differentiate and retrieve temporally separated events. Specifically, we prompted models with sequences containing multiple presentations of the same token, which reappears at the sequence end. By fixing the positions of these repeated tokens and permuting all others, we removed semantic confounds and isolated temporal effects on next-token prediction. Across diverse sequences, models consistently placed the highest probabilities on tokens following a repeated token, but with a notable bias for those nearest the beginning or end of the input. An ablation experiment linked this phenomenon in transformers to induction heads. Extending the analysis to unique semantic contexts with partial overlap further demonstrated that memories embedded in the middle of a prompt are retrieved less reliably. Despite architectural differences, state-space and transformer models showed comparable temporal biases. Our findings deepen the understanding of temporal biases in in-context learning and offer an illustration of how these biases can enable temporal separation and episodic retrieval.

papers.title: Self-Attention Limits Working Memory Capacity of Transformer-Based Models
papers.research_question: Why do transformer-based models exhibit working memory capacity limits in N-back tasks? The paper hypothesizes that the self-attention mechanism is responsible.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the self-attention mechanism in transformers limits working memory capacity, as increased task difficulty (larger N) leads to higher entropy in attention scores and lower accuracy, analogous to human attention limits.
papers.conclusion: The self-attention mechanism in transformers is both essential for performing the N-back task and responsible for its working memory capacity limits, mirroring the role of selective attention in human cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer model performance on N-back tasks declines as N increases, similar to human working memory limits.
During training, attention scores learn to focus on the N-back position, but this focus becomes less precise as N increases.
Accuracy at a given position is positively correlated with the attention score at the corresponding N-back position.
The total entropy of the attention score matrix increases with N, indicating greater dispersion of attention and lower accuracy.
Even models with more layers and heads show a slight decline in accuracy with increasing N, suggesting a fundamental limit.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified Transformer model without FFNs and layer normalization, limiting direct comparison to pre-trained LLMs.
future_direction: Explore a formal mathematical proof for capacity limits in complex intelligent systems.
Investigate how model architecture complexity and number of parameters affect task performance.
Study the impact of training data amount and hyperparameters on model behavior.
papers.abstract: Recent work on Transformer-based large language models (LLMs) has revealed striking limits in their working memory capacity, similar to what has been found in human behavioral studies. Specifically, these models' performance drops significantly on N-back tasks as N increases. However, there is still a lack of mechanistic interpretability as to why this phenomenon would arise. Inspired by the executive attention theory from behavioral sciences, we hypothesize that the self-attention mechanism within Transformer-based models might be responsible for their working memory capacity limits. To test this hypothesis, we train vanilla decoder-only transformers to perform N-back tasks and find that attention scores gradually aggregate to the N-back positions over training, suggesting that the model masters the task by learning a strategy to pay attention to the relationship between the current position and the N-back position. Critically, we find that the total entropy of the attention score matrix increases as N increases, suggesting that the dispersion of attention scores might be the cause of the capacity limit observed in N-back tasks. Our findings thus offer insights into the shared role of attention in both human and artificial intelligence. Moreover, the limitations of the self-attention mechanism revealed in the current study could inform future efforts to design more powerful model architectures with enhanced working memory capacity and cognitive capabilities.

papers.title: VisQA: X-raying Vision and Language Reasoning in Transformers
papers.research_question: Does a trained model for Visual Question Answering resort to reasoning or to bias exploitation to provide its answer?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces VisQA, an interactive visual analytics tool for instance-based analysis of attention in transformer-based VQA models to investigate reasoning versus bias exploitation.
papers.conclusion: VisQA is an effective interactive tool for in-depth analysis of the reasoning behavior of transformer neural networks for vision and language reasoning, particularly in visual question answering.
papers.key_findings:
VisQA enables experts to analyze attention heads and their functions, helping to identify whether a model is reasoning or exploiting biases.
The tool allows pruning of attention heads and asking free-form questions to test model behavior interactively.
Case studies with VisQA revealed that some attention heads specialize in associating specific words with visual objects (e.g., color words).
The tool's design and evaluation show it makes the inner workings of transformer models more accessible to users.
papers.limitation: VisQA is currently limited to detector-based VL transformers and may face scalability issues with larger models or pixel-based models due to screen real-estate and heatmap complexity.
future_direction: Adapt VisQA to other problems involving transformers, such as machine translation.
Enhance the comparison functionality of VisQA with better visual encoding and more intuitive interactions.
Investigate the role of each attention head in more detail, similar to prior work in NLP.
papers.abstract: Visual Question Answering systems target answering open-ended textual questions given input images. They are a testbed for learning high-level reasoning with a primary use in HCI, for instance assistance for the visually impaired. Recent research has shown that state-of-the-art models tend to produce answers exploiting biases and shortcuts in the training data, and sometimes do not even look at the input image, instead of performing the required reasoning steps. We present VisQA, a visual analytics tool that explores this question of reasoning vs. bias exploitation. It exposes the key element of state-of-the-art neural models - attention maps in transformers. Our working hypothesis is that reasoning steps leading to model predictions are observable from attention distributions, which are particularly useful for visualization. The design process of VisQA was motivated by well-known bias examples from the fields of deep learning and vision-language reasoning and evaluated in two ways. First, as a result of a collaboration of three fields, machine learning, vision and language reasoning, and data analytics, the work lead to a better understanding of bias exploitation of neural models for VQA, which eventually resulted in an impact on its design and training through the proposition of a method for the transfer of reasoning patterns from an oracle model. Second, we also report on the design of VisQA, and a goal-oriented evaluation of VisQA targeting the analysis of a model decision process from multiple experts, providing evidence that it makes the inner workings of models accessible to users.

papers.title: Decoupling Positional and Symbolic Attention Behavior in Transformers
papers.research_question: What are the mathematical properties underlying positional and symbolic attention behaviors? How can we measure them? How do they relate to RoPE frequencies? How does model performance depend on frequency choices?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a theoretical and empirical framework to decouple positional and symbolic attention behaviors in Transformers with RoPE. It introduces a metric to quantify these behaviors and shows how they relate to frequency use, demonstrating that model performance on positional vs. symbolic tasks can be controlled by frequency access.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a detailed understanding of RoPE and how its properties relate to model behavior, decoupling positional and symbolic attention mechanisms and showing they are in tension, with model accuracy depending on the ability to employ appropriate frequencies.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in RoPE-based Transformers exhibit a strong correspondence between behavior and frequency use: lower frequencies are used for symbolic behavior, higher frequencies for positional behavior.
Positional and symbolic behaviors are mutually exclusive (positional-symbolic exclusion principle).
The paper introduces a metric to quantify positional and symbolic scores, enabling visualization of the positional-symbolic profile of a model.
Model performance on canonical tasks (index and information retrieval) depends on the frequencies available: positional tasks require higher frequencies, symbolic tasks require lower frequencies.
Controlling which frequencies attention heads can access allows control over model performance on these tasks.
future_direction: Extend analysis to a wider set of tasks and models
Investigate whether positional and symbolic behaviors are fundamental building blocks of attention heads
papers.abstract: An important aspect subtending language understanding and production is the ability to independently encode positional and symbolic information of the words within a sentence. In Transformers, positional information is typically encoded using Positional Encodings (PEs). One such popular PE, namely Rotary PE (RoPE), has been widely used due to its empirical success. Recently, it has been argued that part of RoPE's success emerges from its ability to encode robust positional and semantic information using large and small frequencies, respectively. In this work, we perform a deeper dive into the positional versus symbolic dichotomy of attention heads behavior, both at the theoretical and empirical level. We provide general definitions of what it means for a head to behave positionally or symbolically, prove that these are two mutually exclusive behaviors and develop a metric to quantify them. We apply our framework to analyze Transformer-based LLMs using RoPE and find that all heads exhibit a strong correspondence between behavior and frequency use. Finally, we introduce canonical tasks designed to be either purely positional or symbolic, and demonstrate that the Transformer performance causally relates to the ability of attention heads to leverage the appropriate frequencies. In particular, we show that we can control the Transformer performance by controlling which frequencies the attention heads can access. Altogether, our work provides a detailed understanding of RoPE, and how its properties relate to model behavior.

papers.title: From Cognition to Computation: A Comparative Review of Human Attention and Transformer Architectures
papers.research_question: What are the similarities and differences between human attention and attention in Transformer architectures, and how can insights from human attention inform the development of more generalized artificial intelligence?
papers.core_contribution: This review provides a comparative analysis of human attention and Transformer attention mechanisms, identifying key similarities and differences, and proposes open research questions for integrating insights from human attention into AI.
papers.conclusion: The review compares human attention and Transformer attention, highlighting similarities and differences, and suggests that insights from human attention can guide the development of more generalized AI, while acknowledging the unique strengths of Transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
Human attention and Transformer attention both involve selective attention, focusing on relevant information while filtering out irrelevant information.
Both human attention and Transformer attention involve contextual understanding, integrating context to interpret information.
Human attention has capacity constraints (limited working memory, sequential processing) while Transformers can process all inputs in parallel without such constraints.
Human attention involves top-down (goal-directed) and bottom-up (stimulus-driven) pathways, while Transformer attention is purely data-driven.
Human attention is intentional and tied to agency and social cognition, while Transformer attention is a mathematical construct without inherent cognitive states.
papers.limitation: The article is not an exhaustive review of either human attention or Transformer architecture, but a focused comparative analysis.
future_direction: Is emulating human capacity constraints beneficial?
How can models adopt a resource-rational approach from human attention?
How can attention modeling generate meaningful representations?
How can attention be formulated as an explicit component of agency?
papers.abstract: Attention is a cornerstone of human cognition that facilitates the efficient extraction of information in everyday life. Recent developments in artificial intelligence like the Transformer architecture also incorporate the idea of attention in model designs. However, despite the shared fundamental principle of selectively attending to information, human attention and the Transformer model display notable differences, particularly in their capacity constraints, attention pathways, and intentional mechanisms. Our review aims to provide a comparative analysis of these mechanisms from a cognitive-functional perspective, thereby shedding light on several open research questions. The exploration encourages interdisciplinary efforts to derive insights from human attention mechanisms in the pursuit of developing more generalized artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Analyzing the Structure of Attention in a Transformer Language Model
papers.research_question: Does attention align with syntactic dependency relations? Which attention heads attend to which part-of-speech tags? How does attention capture long-distance relationships versus short-distance ones?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes attention in the GPT-2 Transformer language model, finding that attention heads specialize in particular part-of-speech tags at different layers, attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in middle layers, and the deepest layers capture the most distant relationships.
papers.conclusion: The structure of attention in GPT-2 is closely tied to the language modeling objective, with attention patterns often focusing on words relevant for predicting the next token. The analysis provides human-interpretable descriptions of model behavior and is complementary to linguistic probing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Attention targets different parts of speech at different layer depths within the model.
Attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in the middle layers.
The deepest layers of the model capture the most distant relationships.
Attention heads exhibit specific patterns, such as focusing on acronyms, place names, or head nouns, as revealed by exemplar sentences.
Attention variability distinguishes content-dependent from content-independent (position-based) heads.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Wikipedia text, which has a specific encyclopedic format and style, so it is unclear how attention patterns manifest in other types of content.
Attention may not fully explain individual model predictions, as noted by recent work (Jain and Wallace, 2019).
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other Transformer models such as BERT, which has a bidirectional architecture and is trained on both token-level and sentence-level tasks.
Analyze attention patterns in other types of content, such as dialog scripts or song lyrics.
Analyze attention patterns in longer texts, especially for new Transformer variants like Transformer-XL and Sparse Transformer.
papers.abstract: The Transformer is a fully attention-based alternative to recurrent networks that has achieved state-of-the-art results across a range of NLP tasks. In this paper, we analyze the structure of attention in a Transformer language model, the GPT-2 small pretrained model. We visualize attention for individual instances and analyze the interaction between attention and syntax over a large corpus. We find that attention targets different parts of speech at different layer depths within the model, and that attention aligns with dependency relations most strongly in the middle layers. We also find that the deepest layers of the model capture the most distant relationships. Finally, we extract exemplar sentences that reveal highly specific patterns targeted by particular attention heads.

papers.title: Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge, and how does grokking enable this? What are the differences in systematic generalization between composition and comparison tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge through grokking, but systematic generalization varies: composition fails out-of-distribution while comparison succeeds. Mechanistic analysis reveals the formation of generalizing circuits and explains the differences, guiding data and training setups and suggesting architectural improvements.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of learning implicit reasoning through grokking, but the level of systematic generalization depends on the task and the circuit configuration. The findings guide data and training setups and suggest improvements to the transformer architecture for better cross-layer memory sharing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can learn implicit reasoning only through grokking (extended training far beyond overfitting).
The speed of grokking correlates with the ratio of inferred to atomic facts (data distribution), not the absolute training data size.
For composition, transformers fail to generalize systematically to out-of-distribution examples, while for comparison, they succeed.
Mechanistic analysis reveals distinct generalizing circuits: for composition, a sequential circuit that stores atomic facts in separate layers; for comparison, a parallel circuit that stores atomic facts in the same layer.
In a complex reasoning task with a large search space, a fully grokked transformer achieves near-perfect accuracy, while state-of-the-art LLMs with non-parametric memory (GPT-4-Turbo, Gemini-1.5-Pro) fail regardless of prompting or retrieval augmentation.
papers.limitation:
The task formulation (induction and application of inference rules from atomic and inferred facts) may not apply to the full spectrum of reasoning types.
The study is limited to synthetic tasks and may not fully capture real-world reasoning complexities.
future_direction: Developing cross-layer memory-sharing mechanisms for transformers (e.g., memory-augmentation, explicit recurrence) to improve systematic generalization.
Investigating the tradeoff between parametric and non-parametric memory in language models.
Understanding the role of verbalizations (e.g., chain-of-thought) in teaching models to reason implicitly.
papers.abstract: We study whether transformers can learn to implicitly reason over parametric knowledge, a skill that even the most capable language models struggle with. Focusing on two representative reasoning types, composition and comparison, we consistently find that transformers can learn implicit reasoning, but only through grokking, i.e., extended training far beyond overfitting. The levels of generalization also vary across reasoning types: when faced with out-of-distribution examples, transformers fail to systematically generalize for composition but succeed for comparison. We delve into the model's internals throughout training, conducting analytical experiments that reveal: 1) the mechanism behind grokking, such as the formation of the generalizing circuit and its relation to the relative efficiency of generalizing and memorizing circuits, and 2) the connection between systematicity and the configuration of the generalizing circuit. Our findings guide data and training setup to better induce implicit reasoning and suggest potential improvements to the transformer architecture, such as encouraging cross-layer knowledge sharing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a challenging reasoning task with a large search space, GPT-4-Turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro based on non-parametric memory fail badly regardless of prompting styles or retrieval augmentation, while a fully grokked transformer can achieve near-perfect accuracy, showcasing the power of parametric memory for complex reasoning.

papers.title: An Adversarial Example for Direct Logit Attribution: Memory Management in GELU-4L
papers.research_question: Does memory management (erasure) occur in transformers, and how does it affect the interpretation of model components via direct logit attribution?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides concrete evidence for memory management (erasure) in a 4-layer transformer and demonstrates that direct logit attribution (DLA) can yield misleading results when erasure is present.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the need for caution when using DLA, as erasure can lead to misleading results. The authors recommend testing effects across varied prompts and complementing DLA with activation patching.
papers.key_findings:
The output of attention head L0H2 is erased by later attention heads in layer 2.
The erasure behavior is causally dependent on V-composition between the writing and erasing heads.
DLA contributions of the writing head and erasing heads are highly anti-correlated, indicating DLA can overstate the writing head's contribution.
Adversarial examples show high DLA values for the writing head even when its input is patched, indicating the DLA signal is not genuine.
papers.limitation: The study focused on a single model and a specific attention head, so the generalizability of the phenomena to other components and model sizes is unclear.
papers.abstract: Prior work suggests that language models manage the limited bandwidth of the residual stream through a "memory management" mechanism, where certain attention heads and MLP layers clear residual stream directions set by earlier layers. Our study provides concrete evidence for this erasure phenomenon in a 4-layer transformer, identifying heads that consistently remove the output of earlier heads. We further demonstrate that direct logit attribution (DLA), a common technique for interpreting the output of intermediate transformer layers, can show misleading results by not accounting for erasure.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a mechanism in Transformer-based LMs for arithmetic reasoning: information is transferred via attention to the last token and processed by late MLP modules to incorporate result-related information into the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides empirical evidence that LMs process arithmetic queries by conveying information via attention to the last token, where late MLPs generate result-related information, and this mechanism is specific to arithmetic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Early MLP layers at operand tokens encode operand information, while attention modules transfer this information to the last token.
Late MLP modules at the last token encode result-related information and incorporate it into the residual stream.
This activation pattern is specific to arithmetic queries compared to number retrieval and factual knowledge tasks.
Fine-tuning on three-operand queries leads to the emergence of the late MLP activation site observed in two-operand settings.
Neuron-level interventions show that the circuits for arithmetic are distinct from those for other tasks.
papers.limitation:
The scope is limited to the four fundamental arithmetic operators (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division).
Queries are synthetically-generated from natural language descriptions rather than real-life math word problems.
Attention modules are considered as a whole without analyzing individual attention heads.
future_direction: Studying a broader set of mathematical operators.
Expanding analysis to math-based queries in real-life settings.
Identifying specific attention heads responsible for information transfer.
papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: SelfIE: Self-Interpretation of Large Language Model Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the hidden embeddings of large language models in natural language to reveal their internal reasoning and enable control over model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SelfIE, a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own hidden embeddings in natural language, and extends it to control model behavior via supervised and reinforcement control on embeddings.
papers.conclusion: SelfIE provides a powerful framework for interpreting and controlling LLM reasoning by generating text descriptions of hidden embeddings, opening avenues for transparent and reliable model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SelfIE can elicit implicit world state knowledge in embeddings without training, matching the performance of a 100-shot linear probe.
SelfIE reveals internal reasoning processes behind complex LLM behaviors such as harmful knowledge recall, prompt injection, ethical decisions, physics reasoning, social reasoning, and hallucination.
SelfIE-based supervised control can edit fact associations and open-ended concepts with good generalization, requiring gradient computation only for individual layers.
SelfIE-based reinforcement control can erase harmful knowledge in LLMs without supervised targets, reducing prompt injection success rate by 84.66%.
SelfIE-based control can override user-specified ethical preferences, increasing fairness in LLM responses with a 95% effective rate.
future_direction: Further exploration of reasoning patterns in LLMs and model reasoning behavior controls with hidden embeddings.
papers.abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) obtain their answers? The ability to explain and control an LLM's reasoning process is key for reliability, transparency, and future model developments. We propose SelfIE (Self-Interpretation of Embeddings), a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own embeddings in natural language by leveraging their ability to respond to inquiries about a given passage. Capable of interpreting open-world concepts in the hidden embeddings, SelfIE reveals LLM internal reasoning in cases such as making ethical decisions, internalizing prompt injection, and recalling harmful knowledge. SelfIE's text descriptions on hidden embeddings also open up new avenues to control LLM reasoning. We propose Supervised Control, which allows editing open-ended concepts while only requiring gradient computation of individual layer. We extend RLHF to hidden embeddings and propose Reinforcement Control that erases harmful knowledge in LLM without supervision targets.

papers.title: Probabilistic Reasoning with Transformer Networks: An Application to Predicate Judgment
papers.research_question: Can transformer networks (BERT) model human semantic judgments for both atomic and compound sentences, and can a probabilistic reasoning model that aggregates BERT's judgments better capture human evaluations of compound sentences?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer networks (BERT) model human judgments for atomic sentences but fail for compound sentences; a Probabilistic Reasoner that aggregates BERT's judgments using probability theory better captures human evaluations of compound sentences.
papers.conclusion: Probabilistic reasoning rules can be applied to BERT's outputs to model complex predicate judgment, integrating neural network modeling with probabilistic cognitive modeling to study naturalistic high-level cognition.
papers.key_findings:
BERT performs well on atomic sentences but fails to process negations and has difficulty with conditionals.
The Probabilistic Reasoner outperforms BERT and a bag-of-words similarity model in predicting human ratings for compound sentences.
The Probabilistic Reasoner captures asymmetries in conditional judgments and differences between conjunctions and disjunctions.
The Probabilistic Reasoner does not account for conjunction and disjunction fallacies, which are captured by BERT and the bag-of-words model.
Human semantic judgment may involve both associative (neural network) and deliberative (probabilistic reasoning) processes.
papers.limitation:
The Probabilistic Reasoner is unable to predict the emergence of the conjunction and disjunction fallacies.
The stimuli were not designed to distinguish between different types of probabilistic models.
future_direction: Extend the approach to more complex types of thinking (deductive reasoning, feature induction).
Use process-level accounts (serial and parallel processes) from response time data.
Test alternative probabilistic rules to explain fallacies.
papers.abstract: Transformer networks that are trained on participant-generated feature norms have been shown to replicate several behavioral patterns observed in prior research on human semantic cognition. In this paper, I compare the predictions of these networks with participant evaluations of sentences sampled from a vast domain of discourse, with thousands of naturalistic predicates. I find that existing transformer networks make human-like predictions when given atomic sentences. However, they fail to capture participant evaluations of compound sentences with conjunctions, disjunctions, negations, and conditionals. Instead, participant responses are best captured by a Probabilistic Reasoner, which aggregates transformer judgments according to the rules of probability theory. These results suggest that human semantic cognition may also rely on a combination of associative processes and deliberative processes when judging complex statements about the world. In doing so they show how probabilistic cognitive modeling and neural network modeling can be integrated to study naturalistic high-level cognition.

papers.title: On the Importance of Local Information in Transformer Based Models
papers.research_question: Can all attention heads in Transformer-based models be constrained to be local without affecting performance? The paper investigates whether local attention alone is sufficient for high accuracy on NLP tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer-based models can be constrained to use only local attention without significant performance drop, and that local attention is sufficient for high accuracy on NLP tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that local attention is sufficient for accurate Transformer-based models, and that constraining attention to be local can be combined with parameter sharing while preserving high accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Sensitivity analysis shows that token representations are more sensitive to local tokens than to syntactically related distant tokens.
Attention bias metric reveals that a larger fraction of attention heads have a locality bias compared to a syntactic bias.
Models with all attention heads constrained to be local achieve comparable performance to unconstrained models on machine translation and GLUE tasks.
Parameter sharing among local attention heads can be done without significant performance drop, especially when untying the last few layers.
Constraining attention to be local can reduce model size and computational cost while maintaining accuracy.
future_direction: More efficient implementation of local attention
Analysis of compute efficiency
papers.abstract: The self-attention module is a key component of Transformer-based models, wherein each token pays attention to every other token. Recent studies have shown that these heads exhibit syntactic, semantic, or local behaviour. Some studies have also identified promise in restricting this attention to be local, i.e., a token attending to other tokens only in a small neighbourhood around it. However, no conclusive evidence exists that such local attention alone is sufficient to achieve high accuracy on multiple NLP tasks. In this work, we systematically analyse the role of locality information in learnt models and contrast it with the role of syntactic information. More specifically, we first do a sensitivity analysis and show that, at every layer, the representation of a token is much more sensitive to tokens in a small neighborhood around it than to tokens which are syntactically related to it. We then define an attention bias metric to determine whether a head pays more attention to local tokens or to syntactically related tokens. We show that a larger fraction of heads have a locality bias as compared to a syntactic bias. Having established the importance of local attention heads, we train and evaluate models where varying fractions of the attention heads are constrained to be local. Such models would be more efficient as they would have fewer computations in the attention layer. We evaluate these models on 4 GLUE datasets (QQP, SST-2, MRPC, QNLI) and 2 MT datasets (En-De, En-Ru) and clearly demonstrate that such constrained models have comparable performance to the unconstrained models. Through this systematic evaluation we establish that attention in Transformer-based models can be constrained to be local without affecting performance.

papers.title: Talking Heads: Understanding Inter-layer Communication in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: How is information represented and routed between layers in transformer language models, specifically through low-rank communication channels?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LMs use low-rank subspaces (communication channels) in the residual stream to pass information between layers; these channels can be identified via SVD of weight matrices and are causally important for model behaviors.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn intricately structured representations through pretraining, and the discovered communication channels provide a mechanistic explanation for some prompt sensitivities, enabling improved model performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer LMs use low-rank (1D or 2D) subspaces in the residual stream for inter-layer communication.
These communication channels can be identified by applying SVD to weight matrices (OV and QK) and computing composition scores on the rank-1 components.
The identified channels are causally important for model behaviors, such as inhibition in the IOI task.
The model's sensitivity to item order in a list (Laundry List task) is explained by the limited capacity of these low-rank channels.
Model editing (zeroing or scaling components) based on these channels can significantly improve performance on the Laundry List task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not work for key composition (Appendix B).
Analysis is limited to two small models (GPT-2 small and Pythia 160m).
Difficulty in controlling all variables in the available data (Section 7).
future_direction: Future work in static weight analysis more generally.
More rigorous analysis of interactions between specific heads (e.g., 8.3 and 9.9).
Extending the method to analyze more complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: Although it is known that transformer language models (LMs) pass features from early layers to later layers, it is not well understood how this information is represented and routed by the model. We analyze a mechanism used in two LMs to selectively inhibit items in a context in one task, and find that it underlies a commonly used abstraction across many context-retrieval behaviors. Specifically, we find that models write into low-rank subspaces of the residual stream to represent features which are then read out by later layers, forming low-rank communication channels (Elhage et al., 2021) between layers. A particular 3D subspace in model activations in GPT-2 can be traversed to positionally index items in lists, and we show that this mechanism can explain an otherwise arbitrary-seeming sensitivity of the model to the order of items in the prompt. That is, the model has trouble copying the correct information from context when many items ``crowd" this limited space. By decomposing attention heads with the Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that previously described interactions between heads separated by one or more layers can be predicted via analysis of their weight matrices alone. We show that it is possible to manipulate the internal model representations as well as edit model weights based on the mechanism we discover in order to significantly improve performance on our synthetic Laundry List task, which requires recall from a list, often improving task accuracy by over 20%. Our analysis reveals a surprisingly intricate interpretable structure learned from language model pretraining, and helps us understand why sophisticated LMs sometimes fail in simple domains, facilitating future analysis of more complex behaviors.

papers.title: The mechanistic basis of data dependence and abrupt learning in an in-context classification task
papers.research_question: What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning, and what is the mechanistic basis of the abrupt transition observed during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that data distributional dependencies for in-context learning are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network, and that the abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, which is explained by a phenomenological model with nested logits.
papers.conclusion: The abrupt transition in ICL is due to the sequential learning of three nested logits in the induction head, and an intrinsic curriculum (slow learning of a simpler strategy) may be necessary to guide the network towards the ICL solution.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing burstiness (B) and number of classes (K) promotes ICL while decreasing IWL.
Within-class variation (ε) promotes ICL and decreases IWL.
A Zipfian rank-frequency distribution (α=1) promotes both ICL and IWL simultaneously.
The network can learn both ICL and IWL solutions simultaneously when trained on a mix of sequences.
The abrupt transition in ICL is driven by the formation of an induction head, preceded by a slow learning phase where the network learns to randomly pick a contextual label.
papers.limitation:
The model is minimal and larger models may use different mechanisms than the ones identified.
The analysis did not use heuristics such as weight tying, which are common in LLMs and might change the learning dynamics.
future_direction: Testing the hypothesis that learning of simpler ICL operations enables the learning of more complex ICL strategies in large language models.
Using methods for mechanistic interpretability to probe these mechanisms in LLMs.
Exploring the role of curricula for accelerating ICL in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Transformer models exhibit in-context learning: the ability to accurately predict the response to a novel query based on illustrative examples in the input sequence. In-context learning contrasts with traditional in-weights learning of query-output relationships. What aspects of the training data distribution and architecture favor in-context vs in-weights learning? Recent work has shown that specific distributional properties inherent in language, such as burstiness, large dictionaries and skewed rank-frequency distributions, control the trade-off or simultaneous appearance of these two forms of learning. We first show that these results are recapitulated in a minimal attention-only network trained on a simplified dataset. In-context learning (ICL) is driven by the abrupt emergence of an induction head, which subsequently competes with in-weights learning. By identifying progress measures that precede in-context learning and targeted experiments, we construct a two-parameter model of an induction head which emulates the full data distributional dependencies displayed by the attention-based network. A phenomenological model of induction head formation traces its abrupt emergence to the sequential learning of three nested logits enabled by an intrinsic curriculum. We propose that the sharp transitions in attention-based networks arise due to a specific chain of multi-layer operations necessary to achieve ICL, which is implemented by nested nonlinearities sequentially learned during training.

papers.title: Mechanistically analyzing the effects of fine-tuning on procedurally defined tasks
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning alter the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining? Does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning rarely alters a model's underlying capabilities; instead, it typically learns a minimal 'wrapper' transformation on top of existing capabilities. These wrapped capabilities can be sample-efficiently revived via further fine-tuning on relevant tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning primarily learns minimal wrapper transformations over existing model capabilities rather than creating or deleting them, which has implications for safety as wrappers can be easily removed or bypassed.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning alters pretraining capabilities by minimally transforming them via a learned 'wrapper'.
Wrappers are often extremely localized; pruning a few neurons can cause the model to revert to its pretraining capability.
Further fine-tuning on a subset of pretraining data leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the original capability.
When a weakly relevant pretraining capability is present, the model exploits spurious correlations in the fine-tuning data via the wrapper.
The presence and strength of a pretraining capability (influenced by its sampling probability during pretraining) significantly affects fine-tuning dynamics and wrapper formation.
papers.limitation: The analysis is conducted primarily in synthetic, controlled settings (Tracr and PCFGs), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world fine-tuning scenarios.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex and realistic tasks and models.
Investigating the societal implications of the findings, particularly regarding the safety of fine-tuned models.
Exploring whether the wrapper phenomenon generalizes to other model adaptation methods beyond standard fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large pre-trained models has become the de facto strategy for developing both task-specific and general-purpose machine learning systems, including developing models that are safe to deploy. Despite its clear importance, there has been minimal work that explains how fine-tuning alters the underlying capabilities learned by a model during pretraining: does fine-tuning yield entirely novel capabilities or does it just modulate existing ones? We address this question empirically in synthetic, controlled settings where we can use mechanistic interpretability tools (e.g., network pruning and probing) to understand how the model's underlying capabilities are changing. We perform an extensive analysis of the effects of fine-tuning in these settings, and show that: (i) fine-tuning rarely alters the underlying model capabilities; (ii) a minimal transformation, which we call a 'wrapper', is typically learned on top of the underlying model capabilities, creating the illusion that they have been modified; and (iii) further fine-tuning on a task where such hidden capabilities are relevant leads to sample-efficient 'revival' of the capability, i.e., the model begins reusing these capability after only a few gradient steps. This indicates that practitioners can unintentionally remove a model's safety wrapper merely by fine-tuning it on a, e.g., superficially unrelated, downstream task. We additionally perform analysis on language models trained on the TinyStories dataset to support our claims in a more realistic setup.

papers.title: Tracing Facts or just Copies? A critical investigation of the Competitions of Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in LLMs mediate the competition between factual recall from parametric memory and counterfactual information provided in context? Do they perform selective counterfactual suppression or general copy suppression, and are they domain-specific?
papers.core_contribution: Attention heads that promote factual output in LLMs operate via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, and their behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models showing more specialization.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that attention heads mediate the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens via copy suppression, and their effects are domain-dependent, with implications for model interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads contribute to the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens, and modifying their strength affects the proportion of factual outputs.
The attention heads supporting factual tokens suppress copying in general, not just counterfactuals, as they also suppress factual tokens when facts are present in the prompt.
The effect of attention heads is sensitive to sentence structure and the presence of hints (factual token in the subject).
Attention heads exhibit domain specialization; their contribution varies by answer category (e.g., location, language, organization).
Larger models (Pythia-6.9B) show more specialized and category-sensitive patterns than smaller models (GPT-2).
papers.limitation: The experiments are limited to two models (GPT-2 and Pythia-6.9B) and do not cover more models or study attention modification of different heads on different domains in detail.
future_direction: Applying the methods to different models
Studying how each attention head interacts with different domains
Constructing new datasets on other domains (e.g., STEM) and applying similar techniques
papers.abstract: This paper presents a reproducibility study examining how Large Language Models (LLMs) manage competing factual and counterfactual information, focusing on the role of attention heads in this process. We attempt to reproduce and reconcile findings from three recent studies by Ortu et al., Yu, Merullo, and Pavlick and McDougall et al. that investigate the competition between model-learned facts and contradictory context information through Mechanistic Interpretability tools. Our study specifically examines the relationship between attention head strength and factual output ratios, evaluates competing hypotheses about attention heads' suppression mechanisms, and investigates the domain specificity of these attention patterns. Our findings suggest that attention heads promoting factual output do so via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, as strengthening them can also inhibit correct facts. Additionally, we show that attention head behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models exhibiting more specialized and category-sensitive patterns.

papers.title: Mechanism and Emergence of Stacked Attention Heads in Multi-Layer Transformers
papers.research_question: What tasks require transformers of a specific depth? Can large language models solve such tasks without fine-tuning? What mechanism do transformers use to solve the task? How does this mechanism emerge during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the retrieval problem, a task requiring a minimum number of transformer layers, and uncovers that transformers solve it using stacked attention heads (retrieval heads) which emerge gradually via an implicit curriculum.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces the retrieval problem, shows it requires a certain number of layers, and finds transformers solve it using a mechanism resembling an induction head that emerges gradually with the help of an implicit curriculum.
papers.key_findings:
The retrieval problem requires a minimum number of transformer layers that grows logarithmically with the number of retrieval steps.
Large language models can solve the retrieval problem without any specific fine-tuning.
Transformers solve the retrieval problem using stacked attention heads that resemble induction heads.
Retrieval heads emerge gradually during training, one head at a time, guided by an implicit curriculum.
The implicit curriculum is essential for successful learning of the retrieval problem.
papers.limitation:
The analysis of transformers trained on a minimal formulation of the retrieval problem might not generalize perfectly to large language models.
The paper does not provide a full explanation of the training dynamics of transformers on the retrieval problem.
future_direction: Further research is needed to fully understand the multi-layered circuits learned by large language models and the training dynamics that enable their learning.
papers.abstract: In this paper, I introduce the retrieval problem, a simple yet common reasoning task that can be solved only by transformers with a minimum number of layers, which grows logarithmically with the input size. I empirically show that large language models can solve the task under different prompting formulations without any fine-tuning. To understand how transformers solve the retrieval problem, I train several transformers on a minimal formulation. Successful learning occurs only under the presence of an implicit curriculum. I uncover the learned mechanisms by studying the attention maps in the trained transformers. I also study the training process, uncovering that attention heads always emerge in a specific sequence guided by the implicit curriculum.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: Is Random Attention Sufficient for Sequence Modeling? Disentangling Trainable Components in the Transformer
papers.research_question: How much, and which aspects, of transformer performance gains can be attributed to the self-attention mechanism, and which degrees of freedom inside the Transformer are truly necessary for its behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers with frozen query and key weights (Frozen-QK) can still form induction heads and perform competitively on language modeling, and that a transformer with entirely random, static attention (MixiT) can perform well on tasks that do not require in-context reasoning, highlighting the distinct roles of attention and MLPs.
papers.conclusion: The transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, and different components (attention and MLPs) are responsible for different capabilities, with attention largely responsible for in-context reasoning and MLPs for memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Frozen-QK, with random attention weights, can form induction heads and achieve competitive language modeling performance.
MixiT, with entirely random static attention, solves algorithmic tasks but fails at tasks requiring in-context reasoning like retrieval.
MLPs are crucial for memorization and collaborate with attention for knowledge storage.
The transformer architecture has an inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits even without learnable attention weights.
MixiT overcomes depth-wise scaling challenges of prior random transformers via stable signal propagation.
papers.limitation: MixiT cannot form input-dependent specialized circuits like induction heads, limiting its performance on tasks requiring in-context reasoning.
future_direction: Further study on why increasing the number of attention heads does not improve performance for some tasks, such as Yelp sentiment classification.
papers.abstract: The transformer architecture is central to the success of modern Large Language Models (LLMs), in part due to its surprising ability to perform a wide range of tasks - including mathematical reasoning, memorization, and retrieval - using only gradient-based learning on next-token prediction. While the core component of a transformer is the self-attention mechanism, we question how much, and which aspects, of the performance gains can be attributed to it. To this end, we compare standard transformers to variants in which either the MLP layers or the attention weights are frozen at initialization. Surprisingly, we find that attention with frozen key and query weights is not only able to form induction heads, but can also perform competitively on language modeling. We formalize this by proving a new expressivity result for transformer models with frozen key and query weights. To further isolate the contribution of attention, we design MixiT, an architecture with entirely random attention scores, with provably stable signal propagation that overcomes prior depth-wise scaling challenges in random transformers. We use the successes and failures of MixiT to understand the role each transformer component plays, such as attention being largely responsible for in-context reasoning, and MLPs being responsible for, but collaborates with attention, on knowledge storage. Our results suggest that the transformer architecture has a built-in inductive bias towards forming specialized circuits, as it does even without learnable attention weights.

papers.title: Complexity Control Facilitates Reasoning-Based Compositional Generalization in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do complexity control strategies like initialization scale and weight decay influence transformers' ability to learn reasoning-based solutions for compositional generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Complexity control strategies, such as small initialization scales and large weight decay, enable transformers to learn reasoning-based solutions for compositional tasks, leading to better out-of-distribution generalization.
papers.conclusion: Complexity control through initialization and weight decay is key to enabling transformers to learn compositional rules and generalize out-of-distribution.
papers.key_findings:
Models exhibit three phases based on initialization: poor generalization, good ID but poor OOD, and good ID and OOD generalization.
Complexity control (small init, large weight decay) promotes reasoning-based solutions with lower complexity bias.
Masking reveals that reasoning-based solutions use key token and anchor information differently.
Neuron condensation and structured embeddings are associated with reasoning phases.
Findings generalize to real-world tasks like image generation and NLP.
papers.abstract: Transformers have demonstrated impressive capabilities across various tasks, yet their performance on compositional problems remains a subject of debate. In this study, we investigate the internal mechanisms underlying Transformers' behavior in compositional tasks. We find that complexity control strategies significantly influence whether the model learns primitive-level rules that generalize out-of-distribution (reasoning-based solutions) or relies solely on memorized mappings (memory-based solutions). By applying masking strategies to the model's information circuits and employing multiple complexity metrics, we reveal distinct internal working mechanisms associated with different solution types. Further analysis reveals that reasoning-based solutions exhibit a lower complexity bias, which aligns with the well-studied neuron condensation phenomenon. This lower complexity bias is hypothesized to be the key factor enabling these solutions to learn reasoning rules. We validate these conclusions across multiple real-world datasets, including image generation and natural language processing tasks, confirming the broad applicability of our findings.

papers.title: Overlap in meaning is a stronger predictor of semantic activation in GPT-3 than in humans
papers.research_question: What are the similarities and differences in semantic activation patterns between GPT-3 and humans, particularly regarding the role of semantic similarity versus associative similarity?
papers.core_contribution: GPT-3's semantic activation patterns are broadly similar to humans, but semantic similarity is a stronger predictor of activation in GPT-3 than associative similarity, unlike in humans where associative similarity plays a larger role.
papers.conclusion: GPT-3's semantic network is organized more around word meaning than co-occurrence, suggesting differences from human semantic memory, but with similarities that can inform psycholinguistic research.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-3 shows higher semantic activation for first-associate word pairs compared to other-associate and unrelated pairs, similar to humans.
GPT-3's semantic activation is more strongly driven by semantic similarity (e.g., synonyms, antonyms) than by associative similarity (e.g., phrasal associates).
Humans show relatively stronger activation for associatively similar words, while GPT-3 shows stronger activation for semantically similar words.
The importance of semantic similarity in predicting activation increases with model complexity and recency.
Differences in measurement approaches (direct cosine similarity vs. indirect reaction times) may contribute to observed disparities.
papers.limitation: Semantic priming effects in humans measured via lexical decision tasks may be affected by processes like expectancy or semantic matching, introducing noise or bias not present in GPT-3's direct measurement.
papers.abstract: Modern large language models generate texts that are virtually indistinguishable from those written by humans and achieve near-human performance in comprehension and reasoning tests. Yet, their complexity makes it difficult to explain and predict their functioning. We examined a state-of-the-art language model (GPT-3) using lexical decision tasks widely used to study the structure of semantic memory in humans. The results of four analyses showed that GPT-3's patterns of semantic activation are broadly similar to those observed in humans, showing significantly higher semantic activation in related (e.g., "lime-lemon") word pairs than in other-related (e.g., "sour-lemon") or unrelated (e.g., "tourist-lemon") word pairs. However, there are also significant differences between GPT-3 and humans. GPT-3's semantic activation is better predicted by similarity in words' meaning (i.e., semantic similarity) rather than their co-occurrence in the language (i.e., associative similarity). This suggests that GPT-3's semantic network is organized around word meaning rather than their co-occurrence in text.

papers.title: Dissecting Persona-Driven Reasoning in Language Models via Activation Patching
papers.research_question: How does assigning a persona influence a language model's reasoning on an objective task, and what are the causal mechanisms within the model that give rise to persona-driven behavior and potential social bias?
papers.core_contribution: Early MLP layers encode persona-specific semantic information, which is then used by middle MHA layers to influence reasoning, and specific attention heads disproportionately attend to racial and color-based identities.
papers.conclusion: The work takes initial steps toward understanding the origins of persona-driven behavior in LLMs and demonstrates how activation patching can pinpoint components that encode and act upon persona-driven biases, offering a pathway for targeted bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Early MLP layers (layers 1-3) process semantic content related to persona, not just syntactic structure, and transform persona tokens into richer representations.
Middle MHA layers (layers 9-11) use the persona information from early MLPs to shape the model's output.
Specific attention heads (e.g., H25_9, H25_10, H26_11) disproportionately attend to tokens representing racial and color-based identities.
Patching activations from early MLP layers (especially at the identity token position) can reduce bias and restore model performance.
The effect of early MLP layers on output is indirect, mediated by later layers.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on Llama 3.2 1B, 3B, and Qwen 1.5B Instruct models, with head-level patching limited to Llama 1B due to computational constraints.
The MMLU dataset is not the only dataset meeting the selection criteria, but it was chosen for its objective, multiple-choice format.
The list of 16 personas is not exhaustive but serves as a practical starting point.
Attention pattern analysis requires manual inspection, which is slow and labor-intensive.
future_direction: Investigate why certain personas answer specific questions correctly while others do not.
Explore how output vector circuits in attention heads use earlier-layer representations to shape final predictions.

papers.title: Semantics-Adaptive Activation Intervention for LLMs via Dynamic Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How can activation intervention methods be made adaptive to the semantic context of inputs, overcoming the limitation of fixed steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes SADI, a dynamic activation intervention method that constructs a steering vector tailored to each input's semantic context, improving task performance without training and generalizing across various LLMs and tasks.
papers.conclusion: SADI advances activation engineering by providing a dynamic and adaptive intervention method that significantly improves model performance across diverse tasks and models without requiring training.
papers.key_findings:
SADI outperforms fixed steering baseline methods (ITI, CAA) by substantial margins across multiple-choice and open-ended generation tasks.
SADI is effective across different model backbones (LLAMA2, BLOOMZ, MISTRAL, FALCON) and model sizes (560M to 7B).
SADI works in few-shot and multilingual settings, demonstrating broad generalizability.
SADI requires only a small number of contrastive pairs (e.g., 150) and no training, making it cost-effective.
Interventions targeting attention heads (SADI-HEAD) consistently yield significant performance improvements across tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance across many tasks, yet aligning them with desired behaviors remains challenging. Activation intervention has emerged as an effective and economical method to modify the behavior of LLMs. Despite considerable interest in this area, current intervention methods exclusively employ a fixed steering vector to modify model activations, lacking adaptability to diverse input semantics. To address this limitation, we propose Semantics-Adaptive Dynamic Intervention (SADI), a novel method that constructs a dynamic steering vector to intervene model activations at inference time. More specifically, SADI utilizes activation differences in contrastive pairs to precisely identify critical elements of an LLM (i.e., attention heads, hidden states, and neurons) for targeted intervention. During inference, SADI dynamically steers model behavior by scaling element-wise activations based on the directions of input semantics. Experimental results show that SADI outperforms established baselines by substantial margins, improving task performance without training. SADI's cost-effectiveness and generalizability across various LLM backbones and tasks highlight its potential as a versatile alignment technique.

papers.title: On the Emergence of Position Bias in Transformers
papers.research_question: How do attention masks and positional encodings shape position bias in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Develops a graph-theoretic framework for analyzing position bias in transformers, revealing that causal masking biases attention toward earlier positions and that relative positional encodings introduce a trade-off between decay effects and cumulative importance of early positions.
papers.conclusion: Our work provides a probabilistic and graph-theoretic framework for understanding position bias in transformers, revealing the inherent bias of causal masks toward earlier tokens and the nuanced interplay with relative positional encodings, offering a foundation for designing attention mechanisms with predictable positional properties.
papers.key_findings:
Causal masking inherently biases attention toward earlier positions in deep networks, as tokens in deeper layers attend to increasingly more contextualized representations of earlier tokens.
The interaction between causal masking and relative positional encodings (e.g., decay mask, RoPE) leads to a trade-off: while they introduce distance-based decay within individual layers, their aggregate effect across layers results in non-monotonic behavior, balancing local decay and cumulative importance of early positions.
Attention sinks emerge as center nodes in the graph defined by the attention mask, explaining why they appear at certain positions (e.g., first token for causal mask, prefix tokens for prefix mask).
The causal mask does not simulate positional encodings but instead introduces a bias toward earlier positions via iterative attention, capturing positional bias only when it aligns with this predisposition.
Residual connections can modulate the accumulation of positional effects across layers, making the relationship between depth and bias non-monotonic.
papers.limitation: The analysis does not extend to other transformer components such as residual connections, value projections, and MLPs, which may interact with attention in nontrivial ways.
future_direction: Leveraging insights to design bias-free transformers, mitigating positional biases to improve model robustness and generalization.
Informing the strategic exploitation of positional bias in specific applications, such as text summarization or recommendation systems.
