Gradual learning of the optimal attention pattern commences during the plateau and precedes the sudden loss drop; intervening on attention maps alters plateau duration and degenerate behaviors.
The phenomena of repetition bias and representation collapse are also observed in the early pre-training stages of large language models like Pythia and OLMo.
future_direction: Understanding why behaviors such as representation collapse exist during early time training.
Rigorous theoretical validation of the 'search' hypothesis and how it connects to task complexity.
papers.abstract: Training Transformers on algorithmic tasks frequently demonstrates an intriguing abrupt learning phenomenon: an extended performance plateau followed by a sudden, sharp improvement. This work investigates the underlying mechanisms for such dynamics, primarily in shallow Transformers. We reveal that during the plateau, the model often develops an interpretable partial solution while simultaneously exhibiting a strong repetition bias in their outputs. This output degeneracy is accompanied by internal representation collapse, where hidden states across different tokens become nearly parallel. We further identify the slow learning of optimal attention maps as a key bottleneck. Hidden progress in attention configuration during the plateau precedes the eventual rapid convergence, and directly intervening on attention significantly alters plateau duration and the severity of repetition bias and representational collapse. We validate that these identified phenomena-repetition bias and representation collapse-are not artifacts of toy setups but also manifest in the early pre-training stage of large language models like Pythia and OLMo.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Rethinking Attention: Exploring Shallow Feed-Forward Neural Networks as an Alternative to Attention Layers in Transformers (Student Abstract)
papers.research_question: Can shallow feed-forward networks effectively mimic and replace attention mechanisms in Transformers for sequence-to-sequence tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Shallow feed-forward networks can effectively replace attention layers in Transformers for translation tasks, rivaling original performance, highlighting their adaptability and potential for streamlining architectures.
papers.conclusion: Empirical evidence shows that 'attentionless Transformers' can achieve comparable performance to original Transformers, indicating attention is not strictly necessary, but current optimization methods require knowledge distillation for training.
papers.key_findings:
Encoder self-attention replacement methods achieve competitive BLEU scores compared to the baseline Transformer.
ALR is the most effective approach for encoder replacement, with high performance and small parameters.
Full Transformer replacement with ALR works well for decoder self-attention but performs worse for cross-attention.
Replacement approaches increase parameter count and reduce flexibility in handling variable sequence lengths.
ELR performs the worst due to simplicity discarding helpful encoder structures.
papers.limitation:
Replacement approaches have more parameters than the original attention layers.
Fixed-size feed-forward networks lack flexibility in handling sequences of different lengths.
Current optimization methods cannot train these attentionless Transformers from scratch without knowledge distillation.
future_direction: Further optimization of feed-forward network hyperparameters using advanced parameter search like Bayesian optimization.
Enabling smaller feed-forward networks for replacement to reduce parameter bottleneck.
papers.abstract: This work presents an analysis of the effectiveness of using standard shallow feed-forward networks to mimic the behavior of the attention mechanism in the original Transformer model, a state-of-the-art architecture for sequence-to-sequence tasks. We substitute key elements of the attention mechanism in the Transformer with simple feed-forward networks, trained using the original components via knowledge distillation. Our experiments, conducted on the IWSLT2017 dataset, reveal the capacity of these ”attentionless Transformers” to rival the performance of the original architecture. Through rigorous ablation studies, and experimenting with various replacement network types and sizes, we offer insights that support the viability of our approach. This not only sheds light on the adaptability of shallow feed-forward networks in emulating attention mechanisms but also underscores their potential to streamline complex architectures for sequence-to-sequence tasks.

papers.title: LayerNorm Induces Recency Bias in Transformer Decoders
papers.research_question: Why do Transformer decoders exhibit recency bias (attention bias toward recent tokens) when prior work shows causal self-attention alone induces a bias toward earlier tokens? How do other architectural components (LayerNorm, residual connections, input embeddings) affect this bias?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LayerNorm, when combined with causal self-attention, induces a recency bias in attention scores in Transformer decoders, and analyzes how residual connections and anisotropic input embeddings modulate this bias.
papers.conclusion: LayerNorm induces recency bias in Transformer decoders, providing insights for improving positional encoding strategies and length generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Stacked causal self-attention layers with LayerNorm induce recency bias, while without LayerNorm they do not.
Residual connections reduce the strength of the recency bias.
Anisotropic input embeddings (high cosine similarity between token embeddings) enhance the recency bias.
The recency bias depends on both query and key positions, not solely on their relative distance.
The theoretical framework extends to modern attention variants like MHA, MQA, and GQA.
papers.limitation:
Does not analyze the effects of feed-forward networks, other learnable parameters, or multi-head attention.
Does not evaluate the relationship between recency bias and overall model performance.
Does not examine the interaction with RoPE positional encoding, which is used in most modern Transformer decoder models.
future_direction: Exploring mitigation strategies, such as modifying the causal mask to counteract the uneven bias.
Design of future positional encoding methods based on these insights.
Research on length generalization in Transformer decoders.
papers.abstract: Causal self-attention provides positional information to Transformer decoders. Prior work has shown that stacks of causal self-attention layers alone induce a positional bias in attention scores toward earlier tokens. However, this differs from the bias toward later tokens typically observed in Transformer decoders, known as recency bias. We address this discrepancy by analyzing the interaction between causal self-attention and other architectural components. We show that stacked causal self-attention layers combined with LayerNorm induce recency bias. Furthermore, we examine the effects of residual connections and the distribution of input token embeddings on this bias. Our results provide new theoretical insights into how positional information interacts with architectural components and suggest directions for improving positional encoding strategies.

papers.title: Shapley Head Pruning: Identifying and Removing Interference in Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: How can interference in multilingual transformers be reduced by identifying and pruning language-specific attention heads?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Shapley Head Pruning, a method to identify and remove language-specific attention heads in multilingual transformers, reducing interference and improving cross-lingual performance without adding parameters.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that Shapley Head Pruning effectively identifies and removes interfering attention heads, improving cross-lingual performance and providing insights into language-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Attention Head Shapley Values exhibit language affinity, with some heads being language-specific and others language-agnostic.
Pruning attention heads with negative Shapley Values improves accuracy on XNLI and UDPOS tasks, with gains up to 24.7%.
Zero-shot pruning using Shapley Values from English can benefit other languages, but not all, indicating transferability.
Language-agnostic attention heads match synonyms across sentences, while language-specific heads have varied behavior.
The method outperforms random pruning and gradient-based baselines in iterative pruning evaluations.
papers.limitation:
Computational cost of Shapley Values is high compared to gradient-based methods.
Reliance on attention visualization for analysis, which may not be a sound analytical tool.
future_direction: Systematically understand relationships between linguistic features, training data volume, and language-specificity of attention heads.
Reduce cross-lingual interference during pre-training, such as pruning during pretraining or utilizing sparsely activated networks.
papers.abstract: Multilingual transformer-based models demonstrate remarkable zero and few-shot transfer across languages by learning and reusing language-agnostic features. However, as a fixed-size model acquires more languages, its performance across all languages degrades, a phenomenon termed interference. Often attributed to limited model capacity, interference is commonly addressed by adding additional parameters despite evidence that transformer-based models are overparameterized. In this work, we show that it is possible to reduce interference by instead identifying and pruning language-specific parameters. First, we use Shapley Values, a credit allocation metric from coalitional game theory, to identify attention heads that introduce interference. Then, we show that removing identified attention heads from a fixed model improves performance for a target language on both sentence classification and structural prediction, seeing gains as large as 24.7\%. Finally, we provide insights on language-agnostic and language-specific attention heads using attention visualization.

papers.title: Do LLMs dream of elephants (when told not to)? Latent concept association and associative memory in transformers
papers.research_question: How robust is fact retrieval in LLMs to context changes, and what does this reveal about associative memory mechanisms in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that fact retrieval in LLMs is not robust and can be hijacked by context, and proposes a synthetic latent concept association task to show transformers implement associative memory via self-attention for aggregation and the value matrix for memory retrieval.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit associative memory behavior, which makes fact retrieval non-robust, and understanding this can help develop more robust models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs are susceptible to context hijacking, where adding context that does not change factual meaning can lead to incorrect fact retrieval.
The latent concept association task models fact retrieval in transformers and shows that transformers can solve it by using self-attention to aggregate information and the value matrix as associative memory.
Theoretical analysis shows that the value matrix is crucial for associative memory and that the embedding space can exhibit a low-rank structure.
In the underparameterized regime, embedding training is necessary for good performance, and the learned embeddings have a structure that relates inner product to Hamming distance.
The attention mechanism can select relevant tokens based on latent clusters, mitigating noise.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to open-source models and may not generalize to commercial models like GPT-4.
The theoretical analysis focuses on single-layer transformers, while multi-layer transformers have more complex behaviors (e.g., induction heads).
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-layer transformers.
Studying more complex associative memory mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have the capacity to store and recall facts. Through experimentation with open-source models, we observe that this ability to retrieve facts can be easily manipulated by changing contexts, even without altering their factual meanings. These findings highlight that LLMs might behave like an associative memory model where certain tokens in the contexts serve as clues to retrieving facts. We mathematically explore this property by studying how transformers, the building blocks of LLMs, can complete such memory tasks. We study a simple latent concept association problem with a one-layer transformer and we show theoretically and empirically that the transformer gathers information using self-attention and uses the value matrix for associative memory.

papers.title: Painless Activation Steering: An Automated, Lightweight Approach for Post-Training Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do there exist activation steering (AS) methods that are both human-independent and adaptive to arbitrary models and arbitrary tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Painless Activation Steering (PAS), a family of fully automated, human-independent methods for activation steering that works with any labeled dataset, removing the need for manual prompt construction or feature annotation.
papers.conclusion: PAS provides a fast, lightweight, and practical automated option for post-training large language models, complementing weight- and prompt-based methods.
papers.key_findings:
PAS reliably improves performance on behavior tasks (bias, morality, alignment) but provides little benefit on intelligence-oriented tasks.
Introspective PAS variants (iPAS) perform best by constructing steering vectors from a model's own errors.
PAS complements existing methods, providing additional gains on top of In-Context Learning (ICL) and outperforming Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on TruthfulQA.
PAS generally does not cause catastrophic forgetting on control tasks, except at very high steering strengths.
PAS is effective even in small data regimes and is computationally and storage efficient compared to weight-based methods.
papers.limitation:
PAS is ineffective on intelligence-oriented tasks that require specialized knowledge or advanced reasoning capacity.
At very high steering strengths, PAS can cause catastrophic forgetting on tasks like Sycophancy and TruthfulQA.
PAS is mathematically equivalent to modifying a single bias vector, which may limit its expressivity compared to methods that update all weights.
future_direction: Extending PAS through multi-task multi-layer composition.
Exploring alternative extraction methods for steering vectors.
Investigating new use cases for the PAS framework.
papers.abstract: Language models (LMs) are typically post-trained for desired capabilities and behaviors via weight-based or prompt-based steering, but the former is time-consuming and expensive, and the latter is not precisely controllable and often requires manual trial-and-error. While activation steering (AS) promises a cheap, fast, and controllable alternative to the two existing post-training methods, current AS techniques require hand-crafted prompt pairs or labor-intensive feature annotation, making them more inconvenient than the plug-and-play methods such as Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). We introduce Painless Activation Steering (PAS), a family of fully automated methods that make AS readily usable with any given labeled dataset, with no need for prompt construction, feature labeling, or human intervention. We evaluate PAS on three open-weight models (Llama3.1-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-8B, and Nous-Hermes-2) and 18 tasks; we find that PAS reliably improves performance for behavior tasks, but not for intelligence-oriented tasks. The introspective variant (iPAS) delivers the strongest causal steering effects (10.1% on Bias, 5.2% on Morality, and 34.8% on Alignment). We also show PAS delivers additional gains on top of In-Context Learning (ICL) and SFT. PAS constructs a fast, lightweight activation vector that can be cheaply trained, easily stored, and activated at will. Our results provide a characterization of where AS helps, where it fails, and how to deploy it as a practical, automated LM post-training option.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: Rethinking Attention: Exploring Shallow Feed-Forward Neural Networks as an Alternative to Attention Layers in Transformers
papers.research_question: Can shallow feed-forward networks effectively mimic and replace attention mechanisms in Transformers for sequence-to-sequence tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Shallow feed-forward networks can be trained via knowledge distillation to replace attention mechanisms in Transformers, achieving comparable performance on machine translation tasks.
papers.conclusion: Empirical evidence shows that Transformers do not necessarily require attention mechanisms, as shallow feed-forward networks can achieve similar performance when trained via knowledge distillation, though current optimization limitations prevent training from scratch.
papers.key_findings:
Shallow feed-forward networks can effectively replace attention layers in Transformers, with the Attention Layer Replacement (ALR) method being the most effective for encoder self-attention.
Decoder self-attention can be successfully replicated, but cross-attention replacement performs worse due to its complexity.
The replacement approaches increase parameter count and reduce flexibility in handling variable sequence lengths.
Knowledge distillation is necessary for training these attentionless Transformers, as current optimization methods cannot train them from scratch.
The viability of feed-forward networks as alternatives to attention mechanisms highlights potential for streamlining complex architectures.
papers.limitation:
Replacement approaches significantly increase the number of parameters.
The fixed-size feed-forward networks lack flexibility in handling sequences of varying lengths.
Cross-attention replacement performs worse due to the complexity of mapping between sequences.
future_direction: Optimizing hyperparameters of feed-forward networks using advanced parameter search like Bayesian optimization.
Training more complex feed-forward networks to better model the cross-attention module.
papers.abstract: This work presents an analysis of the effectiveness of using standard shallow feed-forward networks to mimic the behavior of the attention mechanism in the original Transformer model, a state-of-the-art architecture for sequence-to-sequence tasks. We substitute key elements of the attention mechanism in the Transformer with simple feed-forward networks, trained using the original components via knowledge distillation. Our experiments, conducted on the IWSLT2017 dataset, reveal the capacity of these "attentionless Transformers" to rival the performance of the original architecture. Through rigorous ablation studies, and experimenting with various replacement network types and sizes, we offer insights that support the viability of our approach. This not only sheds light on the adaptability of shallow feed-forward networks in emulating attention mechanisms but also underscores their potential to streamline complex architectures for sequence-to-sequence tasks.

papers.title: If Attention Serves as a Cognitive Model of Human Memory Retrieval, What is the Plausible Memory Representation?
papers.research_question: Investigates whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that Transformer Grammar's attention, operating on syntactic structures, better predicts human reading times than vanilla Transformer, suggesting dual memory representations in human sentence processing with attention as a general memory retrieval algorithm.
papers.conclusion: Attention can serve as the general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from two representational systems, and Transformer Grammar, with its syntactic structure-based attention, best captures dominant factors in human sentence processing.
papers.key_findings:
TG's NAE has stronger predictive power for reading times than Transformer's NAE.
TG's and Transformer's NAE have independent contributions to reading time prediction, suggesting they capture distinct aspects of memory retrieval.
TG's NAE captures interference effects, independent of decay effects modeled by Category Locality Theory.
TG's advantage over TG−comp indicates the importance of treating closed phrases as single representations (via COMPOSE attention) for capturing syntax-based memory retrieval.
The attention mechanism serves as a general algorithm for modeling human memory retrieval from dual representational systems (syntactic and token-based).
papers.limitation:
The NAE calculation procedure (summing across heads, handling subwords) strictly followed Oh and Schuler (2022), but alternative approaches warrant investigation.
The findings are based on the English Natural Stories corpus; generalizability to other languages and cognitive measures (e.g., gaze duration, EEG) remains to be investigated.
The use of 'perfect oracles' for syntactic structures idealizes away from local ambiguities that humans encounter during actual sentence processing.
future_direction: Incorporate more realistic elements such as parallel parsing, left-corner parsing strategies, and memory decay mechanisms to fully operate at the algorithmic level.
Investigate generalizability to different languages and other measures of cognitive load.
Explore alternative approaches to handling layers, attention heads, and subword tokens in NAE calculation.
papers.abstract: Recent work in computational psycholinguistics has revealed intriguing parallels between attention mechanisms and human memory retrieval, focusing primarily on vanilla Transformers that operate on token-level representations. However, computational psycholinguistic research has also established that syntactic structures provide compelling explanations for human sentence processing that token-level factors cannot fully account for. In this paper, we investigate whether the attention mechanism of Transformer Grammar (TG), which uniquely operates on syntactic structures as representational units, can serve as a cognitive model of human memory retrieval, using Normalized Attention Entropy (NAE) as a linking hypothesis between models and humans. Our experiments demonstrate that TG's attention achieves superior predictive power for self-paced reading times compared to vanilla Transformer's, with further analyses revealing independent contributions from both models. These findings suggest that human sentence processing involves dual memory representations -- one based on syntactic structures and another on token sequences -- with attention serving as the general memory retrieval algorithm, while highlighting the importance of incorporating syntactic structures as representational units.

papers.title: Entangled in Representations: Mechanistic Investigation of Cultural Biases in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are cultural biases, such as Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening, internalized and represented within the parameters of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Culturescope, a mechanistic interpretability method to probe internal representations of cultural knowledge, and finds that LLMs internalize Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening, with low-resource cultures being less susceptible due to limited parametric knowledge.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a foundation for future research on mitigating cultural biases and enhancing LLMs' cultural understanding, suggesting that tailored approaches considering both bias and resource levels are needed.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs internalize Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening in their cultural knowledge space.
Low-resource cultures are less susceptible to cultural biases, likely due to the model's limited parametric knowledge about them.
The Cultural Flattening (CF) score and attention contribution scores reveal asymmetric generalization of culturally distinctive knowledge, often aligned with geographic or cultural proximity.
When models answer cultural questions incorrectly, they show a statistically significant preference for biased options (hard negatives) for mid- and high-resource cultures, but not for low-resource cultures.
Culturescope effectively surfaces relevant cultural knowledge from model representations, as validated by relevance evaluation and irrelevant patching tests.
papers.limitation:
Few existing benchmarks are suitable for the evaluation setup, requiring a consistent QA format across cultures; the methods inherit limitations from the benchmarks such as lack of fine-grained cultures and a 1-to-1 mapping of culture and country.
Due to computational constraints, experiments are limited to 8B parameter models.
future_direction: Future work should develop tailored approaches that consider the impact of bias and resource levels to improve LLMs' cultural understanding.
Future research should aim at mitigating internalized cultural biases and developing culturally aligned LLMs.
papers.abstract: The growing deployment of large language models (LLMs) across diverse cultural contexts necessitates a deeper understanding of LLMs' representations of different cultures. Prior work has focused on evaluating the cultural awareness of LLMs by only examining the text they generate. This approach overlooks the internal sources of cultural misrepresentation within the models themselves. To bridge this gap, we propose Culturescope, the first mechanistic interpretability-based method that probes the internal representations of different cultural knowledge in LLMs. We also introduce a cultural flattening score as a measure of the intrinsic cultural biases of the decoded knowledge from Culturescope. Additionally, we study how LLMs internalize cultural biases, which allows us to trace how cultural biases such as Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening emerge within LLMs. We find that low-resource cultures are less susceptible to cultural biases, likely due to the model's limited parametric knowledge. Our work provides a foundation for future research on mitigating cultural biases and enhancing LLMs' cultural understanding.

papers.title: Representation and Pre-Activation of Lexical-Semantic Knowledge in Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: How closely do the intermediate layers of LSTM and transformer language models correspond to human semantic knowledge, both before and after the target word is presented?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer models (GPT-2) are better at capturing semantic knowledge, especially attributive features, than LSTM models, and both models retain rich semantic representations of a concept after it has been presented.
papers.conclusion: The transformer model is much better at capturing attributive features than the LSTM model, whilst both models are able to retain rich semantic representations of the concept after the concept has been given to the network.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer models (GPT-2) outperform LSTM models in capturing semantic knowledge, particularly for attributive features.
Both models retain semantic information about a concept after the word is presented, with earlier layers performing better in the 'after' condition.
The final layer of both models shows a performance drop in the 'after' condition, likely due to increased context specificity.
In the 'before' condition (predicting the word), later layers are more representative of the upcoming word's semantics.
GPT-2's after representations are more effective in lower layers, while JLM's after representations are better in the first layer.
papers.limitation:
The feature pooling method may not fully capture context-specific representations, especially in later layers where representations become more context-specific.
Linear probes may not fully capture the information encoded in the representations; failure to decode a property does not mean it is not encoded.
papers.abstract: Neural network language models have the ability to capture the contextualised meanings of words in a sentence by dynamically evolving a representation of the linguistic input in a manner evocative of human language comprehension. While researchers have been able to analyse whether key linguistic regularities are adequately characterised by these evolving representations, determining whether they activate lexico-semantic knowledge similarly to humans remains challenging. In this paper, we perform a systematic analysis of how closely the intermediate layers from LSTM and transformer language models correspond to human semantic knowledge. Furthermore, in order to make more meaningful comparisons with theories of human language comprehension in psycholinguistics, we focus on two key stages where the meaning of a particular target word may arise: immediately before the word's presentation to the model (comparable to forward inferencing), and immediately after the word token has been input into the network. Our results indicate that the transformer models are better at capturing semantic knowledge relating to lexical concepts, both during word prediction and when retention is required.

papers.title: Intra-neuronal attention within language models Relationships between activation and semantics
papers.research_question: To what extent do neurons in language models exhibit intra-neuronal attention, i.e., a homomorphic relationship between activation segments and categorical segments of tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds a weak but consistent relationship between activation segments and categorical segments in neurons, particularly for tokens with very high activation levels, suggesting a form of intra-neuronal attention.
papers.conclusion: Intra-neuronal attention exists in language model neurons, albeit weakly, and contributes to the progressive formation of high-level categorical abstractions through restructuring in later layers.
papers.key_findings:
Overall categorical homogeneity within activation clusters is low.
Categorical homogeneity increases with activation level: tokens with higher activation tend to be more semantically similar.
The relationship between activation and categorical segments is tenuous and only strong for the highest activation tokens.
Intra-neuronal attention enables categorical restructuring processes in subsequent layers, contributing to higher-level abstractions.
papers.limitation: The use of GPT-2XL embeddings is a specific operational choice that does not represent an absolute semantic ontology, so interpretations are contingent on this particular semantic space.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the ability of perceptron-type neurons in language models to perform intra-neuronal attention; that is, to identify different homogeneous categorical segments within the synthetic thought category they encode, based on a segmentation of specific activation zones for the tokens to which they are particularly responsive. The objective of this work is therefore to determine to what extent formal neurons can establish a homomorphic relationship between activation-based and categorical segmentations. The results suggest the existence of such a relationship, albeit tenuous, only at the level of tokens with very high activation levels. This intra-neuronal attention subsequently enables categorical restructuring processes at the level of neurons in the following layer, thereby contributing to the progressive formation of high-level categorical abstractions.

papers.title: Neural Attention: A Novel Mechanism for Enhanced Expressive Power in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: Can replacing the dot product in transformer attention with a feed-forward network enhance the model's expressive power and predictive performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Neural Attention, a method that replaces the dot product in transformer attention with a feed-forward network to capture nonlinear relationships, demonstrating improved performance on language modeling and image classification tasks.
papers.conclusion: Neural Attention enhances the predictive capabilities of transformers by capturing nonlinear dependencies, and its practical overhead can be managed, making it a promising direction for improving transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
Neural Attention reduces perplexity on WikiText-103 by up to 2.19% compared to standard Dot-Product Attention.
Neural Attention improves validation accuracy on CIFAR-10 by 3.0 percentage points and on CIFAR-100 by 4.26 percentage points.
The computational overhead of Neural Attention can be mitigated by applying it only in the first transformer layer and using linear down-projection of the embedding dimension.
Neural Attention with a down-projection dimension as low as 2 still outperforms Dot-Product Attention, suggesting it is a low-rank operation.
The method is modular and can be integrated into existing transformer architectures with minimal changes.
papers.limitation: Neural Attention introduces higher computational and memory requirements compared to standard Dot-Product Attention.
future_direction: Applying Neural Attention during the pretraining phase of large-scale conversational AI models.
Exploring applications in edge computing where increased performance with minimal efficiency loss is valuable.
Investigating hybrid attention architectures that selectively apply Neural Attention in critical layers to balance efficiency and representational power.
papers.abstract: Transformer models typically calculate attention matrices using dot products, which have limitations when capturing nonlinear relationships between embedding vectors. We propose Neural Attention, a technique that replaces dot products with feed-forward networks, enabling a more expressive representation of relationships between tokens. This approach modifies only the attention matrix calculation while preserving the matrix dimensions, making it easily adaptable to existing transformer-based architectures. We provide a detailed mathematical justification for why Neural Attention increases representational capacity and conduct controlled experiments to validate this claim. When comparing Neural Attention and Dot-Product Attention, NLP experiments on WikiText-103 show a reduction in perplexity of over 2 percent. Similarly, experiments on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 show improvements in accuracy of more than 4 percentage points for image classification tasks. While Neural Attention introduces higher computational demands, we develop techniques to mitigate these challenges, ensuring practical usability without sacrificing the increased expressivity it provides. This work establishes Neural Attention as an effective means of enhancing the predictive capabilities of transformer models across a variety of applications. The code for all experiments is available at https://github.com/awayfromzel/neural-attention-research.

papers.title: Dissecting Recall of Factual Associations in Auto-Regressive Language Models
papers.research_question: How do auto-regressive language models internally retrieve factual associations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-step internal mechanism for factual attribute extraction in auto-regressive LMs, involving subject enrichment by early MLPs, relation propagation, and attribute extraction by attention heads.
papers.conclusion: Factual associations are stored in lower layers and extracted by MLP sublayers to form attribute-rich subject representations; upon a query, the attribute is extracted by MHSA sublayers whose parameters often encode subject-attribute mappings.
papers.key_findings:
Critical information flows from relation and then subject positions to the prediction via specific attention edges.
Subject representations are enriched with multiple attributes by early MLP sublayers.
Attribute extraction is primarily performed by upper MHSA sublayers via attention heads that encode subject-attribute mappings.
The extraction mechanism is a three-step process: subject enrichment, relation propagation, and attribute extraction.
Approximately 70% of predictions use this extraction mechanism.
papers.limitation:
Projections to vocabulary space are an approximation, especially in early layers.
Attention knockout may have information leakage across positions, though blocking a range of layers alleviates this.
future_direction: knowledge localization
model editing
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) are known to capture factual knowledge in their parameters. While previous work looked into where factual associations are stored, only little is known about how they are retrieved internally during inference. We investigate this question through the lens of information flow. Given a subject-relation query, we study how the model aggregates information about the subject and relation to predict the correct attribute. With interventions on attention edges, we first identify two critical points where information propagates to the prediction: one from the relation positions followed by another from the subject positions. Next, by analyzing the information at these points, we unveil a three-step internal mechanism for attribute extraction. First, the representation at the last-subject position goes through an enrichment process, driven by the early MLP sublayers, to encode many subject-related attributes. Second, information from the relation propagates to the prediction. Third, the prediction representation "queries" the enriched subject to extract the attribute. Perhaps surprisingly, this extraction is typically done via attention heads, which often encode subject-attribute mappings in their parameters. Overall, our findings introduce a comprehensive view of how factual associations are stored and extracted internally in LMs, facilitating future research on knowledge localization and editing.

papers.title: Bridging the Knowledge-Prediction Gap in LLMs on Multiple-Choice Questions
papers.research_question: What is the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs on multiple-choice questions and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a geometric interpretation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs and introduces KAPPA, an inference-time intervention that aligns knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream to mitigate the gap.
papers.conclusion: The knowledge-prediction gap is a pervasive phenomenon in LLMs, and representation-level alignment via methods like KAPPA can elicit more faithful predictions.
papers.key_findings:
The knowledge-prediction gap is widespread across diverse MCQ benchmarks and model families.
The gap can be geometrically interpreted as a misalignment between knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream.
KAPPA effectively reduces the gap and improves accuracy across benchmarks without additional training.
The gap is more pronounced in reasoning, truthfulness, and bias benchmarks compared to knowledge-intensive benchmarks.
The identified subspaces partially transfer across tasks requiring similar skills.
papers.limitation: The method relies on linearly accessible knowledge, leaving nonlinearly encoded knowledge unexplored.
future_direction: Developing more reliable methods to extract knowledge from model representations.
Understanding how nonlinearly encoded knowledge can be aligned.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on diverse tasks, their trustworthiness is limited by erratic behavior that is unfaithful to their internal knowledge. In particular, LLMs often fail on multiple-choice questions (MCQs) even if they encode correct answers in their hidden representations, revealing a misalignment between internal knowledge and output behavior. We investigate and mitigate this knowledge-prediction gap on MCQs through a three-step analysis of hidden representations. First, we quantify the prevalence and magnitude of the gap across models and datasets. Second, we provide a geometric interpretation by identifying distinct knowledge and prediction subspaces in the residual stream. Third, we introduce KAPPA, a lightweight inference-time intervention that aligns the two subspaces within the residual stream to reduce the knowledge-prediction gap. Our results provide a geometric and interpretable explanation of the knowledge-prediction gap in LLMs. Furthermore, KAPPA effectively reduces the gap across diverse MCQ benchmarks and models, and generalizes to free-form settings.

papers.title: A Study on How Attention Scores in the BERT Model are Aware of Lexical Categories in Syntactic and Semantic Tasks on the GLUE Benchmark
papers.research_question: Do attention scores in the BERT model significantly vary based on lexical categories during fine-tuning for downstream tasks, with content words emphasized in semantic tasks and function words in syntactic tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an extracting algorithm to show that BERT's attention scores shift based on lexical categories during fine-tuning, with content words emphasized in semantic tasks and function words in syntactic tasks, and reveals task-agnostic layer preferences.
papers.conclusion: The study validates the hypothesis that attention scores in BERT shift based on lexical categories during fine-tuning, and identifies layers with consistent preferences, contributing to understanding attention mechanisms in language processing.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts occur during fine-tuning: function words receive more attention in syntactic tasks (e.g., CoLA), while content words receive more attention in semantic tasks (e.g., WiC).
Certain BERT layers consistently attend more to content words (e.g., layers 1, 10, 11, 12) or function words (e.g., layers 2, 4, 8, 9) across diverse downstream tasks.
The extracting algorithm can decrypt token relationships from attention score matrices without distorting values, enabling layer-wise analysis.
The hypothesis that attention scores vary with lexical categories and task objectives is validated through experiments on GLUE tasks.
Layer-wise analysis demonstrates generalization of attention patterns, indicating BERT layers acquire linguistic knowledge associated with lexical categories.
papers.limitation:
Focus on the BERT-based model and its attention mechanism
Oversimplification of linguistic phenomena using lexical categories as a proxy
Limited generalizability to the specific downstream tasks and dataset used
Subjective interpretation of attention shifts and their implications
papers.abstract: This study examines whether the attention scores between tokens in the BERT model significantly vary based on lexical categories during the fine-tuning process for downstream tasks. Drawing inspiration from the notion that in human language processing, syntactic and semantic information is parsed differently, we categorize tokens in sentences according to their lexical categories and focus on changes in attention scores among these categories. Our hypothesis posits that in downstream tasks that prioritize semantic information, attention scores centered on content words are enhanced, while in cases emphasizing syntactic information, attention scores centered on function words are intensified. Through experimentation conducted on six tasks from the GLUE benchmark dataset, we substantiate our hypothesis regarding the fine-tuning process. Furthermore, our additional investigations reveal the presence of BERT layers that consistently assign more bias to specific lexical categories, irrespective of the task, highlighting the existence of task-agnostic lexical category preferences.

papers.title: How do Transformers Learn Implicit Reasoning?
papers.research_question: How do transformers learn implicit reasoning, specifically multi-hop implicit reasoning, and what are the internal mechanisms that enable this ability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a three-stage developmental trajectory for implicit reasoning in transformers (memorization, in-distribution generalization, cross-distribution generalization) and introduces two diagnostic tools (cross-query semantic patching, cosine-based representational lens) that link representational clustering to reasoning capability.
papers.conclusion: Implicit reasoning in transformers is driven by the clustering of intermediate representations in cosine space, and generalization patterns depend on representational alignment, offering insights into the interpretability of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit reasoning emerges in three distinct stages: memorization, in-distribution generalization, and cross-distribution generalization.
Training with atomic triples accelerates learning but is not strictly necessary for in-distribution generalization.
Second-hop generalization requires query-level exposure to specific compositional structures; exposure to the same fact in other roles is insufficient.
Intermediate entity representations are located in middle layers (e.g., layer 5 at the r1 token) and are not necessarily decodable via logit lens, indicating a gap between explicit decodability and functional usage.
Successful reasoning correlates with cosine-space clustering of intermediate representations; generalization patterns depend on representational alignment driven by in-distribution supervision.
papers.limitation: The study uses a controlled symbolic environment, which is simpler than the rich and complex knowledge bases of real LLMs, so the findings are preliminary and may not fully explain reasoning dynamics in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) can perform multi-hop reasoning implicitly -- producing correct answers without explicitly verbalizing intermediate steps -- but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we study how such implicit reasoning emerges by training transformers from scratch in a controlled symbolic environment. Our analysis reveals a three-stage developmental trajectory: early memorization, followed by in-distribution generalization, and eventually cross-distribution generalization. We find that training with atomic triples is not necessary but accelerates learning, and that second-hop generalization relies on query-level exposure to specific compositional structures. To interpret these behaviors, we introduce two diagnostic tools: cross-query semantic patching, which identifies semantically reusable intermediate representations, and a cosine-based representational lens, which reveals that successful reasoning correlates with the cosine-base clustering in hidden space. This clustering phenomenon in turn provides a coherent explanation for the behavioral dynamics observed across training, linking representational structure to reasoning capability. These findings provide new insights into the interpretability of implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs, helping to clarify how complex reasoning processes unfold internally and offering pathways to enhance the transparency of such models.

papers.title: A Residual-Aware Theory of Position Bias in Transformers
papers.research_question: What are the architectural origins of position bias in Transformers, and how do residual connections prevent the collapse of attention to the first token?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a residual-aware theory of cumulative attention rollout that explains position bias in Transformers, showing residual connections prevent collapse to the first token and induce U-shaped influence profiles.
papers.conclusion: Residual connections are crucial for preventing attention collapse, and the residual-aware theory provides a principled architectural explanation for position bias in Transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Residual connections prevent the collapse of attention to the first token in deep Transformers.
Transformer architecture alone induces broad, often U-shaped influence profiles over input positions, explaining the Lost-in-the-Middle phenomenon.
At infinite depth, attention collapse depends on the cumulative strength of attention mixing and is not inevitable.
Theoretical predictions closely match empirical measurements of input token influence in pre-trained language models.
papers.limitation:
Architectural scope abstracts away training dynamics, optimization, and token semantics.
Positional encodings analysis focuses on ALiBi; RoPE is not fully covered.
Lost-in-the-Middle analysis does not model downstream task performance.
future_direction: Developing tighter finite-depth probes for RoPE positional encodings.
papers.abstract: Transformer models systematically favor certain token positions, yet the architectural origins of this position bias remain poorly understood. Under causal masking at infinite depth, prior theoretical analyses of attention rollout predict an inevitable collapse of attention onto the first token. Such collapse, however, does not occur in practice. We resolve this discrepancy with a residual-aware theory of cumulative attention rollout. By incorporating residual connections, we show that this architectural component prevents collapse under realistic conditions. At finite depth, we prove that causal Transformers induce a U-shaped position bias, with attention concentrating on early and late tokens. This result provides a principled architectural explanation for the Lost-in-the-Middle phenomenon.

papers.title: Contextual modulation of language comprehension in a dynamic neural model of lexical meaning
papers.research_question: How does contextual modulation affect lexical meaning comprehension in a dynamic neural model? The paper investigates the semantic basis of lexical polysemy using the English word 'have' as a test case.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a dynamic neural model of lexical meaning that explains contextual modulation in language comprehension, showing that polysemy arises from transiently stable neural activation states on continuous semantic dimensions.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that lexical polysemy is best explained by continuous neural dynamics on semantic dimensions, rather than by discrete meaning representations.
papers.key_findings:
Model simulations capture contextual modulation of lexical semantic interpretation and individual variation in this modulation.
Simulations generate a novel prediction that the relationship between sentence reading time and acceptability should be contextually modulated.
The behavioral experiment replicates previous results showing higher acceptability and faster reading times for sentences in an adjacency context.
The experiment partially confirms the model's novel prediction regarding the interaction between context and acceptability in reading time.
Individual variation in contextual facilitation is correlated with Autism-Spectrum Quotient scores, supporting the model's account of individual differences.
future_direction: Extend the model to other polysemous words and interpretations beyond the English word 'have'.
papers.abstract: We computationally implement and experimentally test the behavioral predictions of a dynamic neural model of lexical meaning in the framework of Dynamic Field Theory. We demonstrate the architecture and behavior of the model using as a test case the English lexical item have, focusing on its polysemous use. In the model, have maps to a semantic space defined by two independently motivated continuous conceptual dimensions, connectedness and control asymmetry. The mapping is modeled as coupling between a neural node representing the lexical item and neural fields representing the conceptual dimensions. While lexical knowledge is modeled as a stable coupling pattern, real-time lexical meaning retrieval is modeled as the motion of neural activation patterns between transiently stable states corresponding to semantic interpretations or readings. Model simulations capture two previously reported empirical observations: (1) contextual modulation of lexical semantic interpretation, and (2) individual variation in the magnitude of this modulation. Simulations also generate a novel prediction that the by-trial relationship between sentence reading time and acceptability should be contextually modulated. An experiment combining self-paced reading and acceptability judgments replicates previous results and partially bears out the model's novel prediction. Altogether, results support a novel perspective on lexical polysemy: that the many related meanings of a word are not categorically distinct representations; rather, they are transiently stable neural activation states that arise from the nonlinear dynamics of neural populations governing interpretation on continuous semantic dimensions. Our model offers important advantages over related models in the dynamical systems framework, as well as models based on Bayesian inference.

papers.title: Explanation based Bias Decoupling Regularization for Natural Language Inference
papers.research_question: How can we train Transformer-based Natural Language Inference encoders to identify and decouple biased components within each sample (at the word level) to improve out-of-distribution inference, inspired by human explanations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Explanation based Bias Decoupling Regularization (EBD-Reg), a debiasing method that uses human explanations to guide Transformer-based NLI encoders to distinguish and decouple task-relevant keywords from biased words at the token level, significantly improving out-of-distribution inference performance.
papers.conclusion: EBD-Reg effectively trains Transformer-based NLI encoders to decouple biases from task-relevant features using human explanations, significantly outperforming prior debiasing methods on out-of-distribution inference tasks.
papers.key_findings:
EBD-Reg, when combined with Adaptive Token-level Attention (ATA), achieves state-of-the-art out-of-distribution inference performance across multiple NLI benchmarks.
EBD-Reg can be easily integrated with various Transformer-based encoders (BERT, ALBERT, RoBERTa, etc.) without requiring architectural changes or additional inference overhead.
The method's three supervision targets (Distinguishing, Decoupling, Aligning) complement each other, with the full combination yielding the best performance improvement.
Case studies show that EBD-Reg successfully shifts model attention to keywords (nouns, verbs) and away from biased words, leading to more interpretable predictions.
Ablation studies confirm that all three components of EBD-Reg contribute to its effectiveness, with entity recognition (Distinguishing) being crucial for identifying keywords and biases.
papers.abstract: The robustness of Transformer-based Natural Language Inference encoders is frequently compromised as they tend to rely more on dataset biases than on the intended task-relevant features. Recent studies have attempted to mitigate this by reducing the weight of biased samples during the training process. However, these debiasing methods primarily focus on identifying which samples are biased without explicitly determining the biased components within each case. This limitation restricts those methods' capability in out-of-distribution inference. To address this issue, we aim to train models to adopt the logic humans use in explaining causality. We propose a simple, comprehensive, and interpretable method: Explanation based Bias Decoupling Regularization (EBD-Reg). EBD-Reg employs human explanations as criteria, guiding the encoder to establish a tripartite parallel supervision of Distinguishing, Decoupling and Aligning. This method enables encoders to identify and focus on keywords that represent the task-relevant features during inference, while discarding the residual elements acting as biases. Empirical evidence underscores that EBD-Reg effectively guides various Transformer-based encoders to decouple biases through a human-centric lens, significantly surpassing other methods in terms of out-of-distribution inference capabilities.

papers.title: Dissecting Multimodal In-Context Learning: Modality Asymmetries and Circuit Dynamics in modern Transformers
papers.research_question: What enables transformers to perform multimodal ICL, both in terms of training data statistics and mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals a learning asymmetry in multimodal ICL where the primary modality installs the core ICL circuit, enabling multimodal ICL to emerge with low data complexity in the secondary modality.
papers.conclusion: The paper uncovers a learning asymmetry where the primary modality installs the core ICL circuit, enabling multimodal ICL to emerge with low data complexity in the secondary modality.
papers.key_findings:
RoPE increases the data complexity threshold for ICL emergence.
Multimodal ICL exhibits a learning asymmetry: with high-diversity primary modality, surprisingly low data complexity in the secondary modality suffices.
Scaling up unimodal models favors in-weight memorization over ICL, but scaling improves multimodal ICL.
Multimodal ICL relies on induction-style mechanisms that copy labels from matching in-context exemplars.
Encoders improve multimodal ICL by aligning features and providing discriminative representations.
papers.limitation: Observations on production MLLMs are not intended as a mechanistic explanation due to vastly more complex training regimes, data distributions, and architectural choices that confound clean attribution.
future_direction: Investigate circuit-level robustness.
Explore architectural designs that inherently favor robust reasoning over memorization.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based multimodal large language models often exhibit in-context learning (ICL) abilities. Motivated by this phenomenon, we ask: how do transformers learn to associate information across modalities from in-context examples? We investigate this question through controlled experiments on small transformers trained on synthetic classification tasks, enabling precise manipulation of data statistics and model architecture. We begin by revisiting core principles of unimodal ICL in modern transformers. While several prior findings replicate, we find that Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) increases the data complexity threshold for ICL. Extending to the multimodal setting reveals a fundamental learning asymmetry: when pretrained on high-diversity data from a primary modality, surprisingly low data complexity in the secondary modality suffices for multimodal ICL to emerge. Mechanistic analysis shows that both settings rely on an induction-style mechanism that copies labels from matching in-context exemplars; multimodal training refines and extends these circuits across modalities. Our findings provide a mechanistic foundation for understanding multimodal ICL in modern transformers and introduce a controlled testbed for future investigation.

papers.title: From Concepts to Components: Concept-Agnostic Attention Module Discovery in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we map arbitrary, complex concepts to specific attention heads in transformer models in a concept-agnostic way, and how can we intervene on these modules to control model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a concept-agnostic method (SAMD) to map arbitrary concepts to sparse sets of attention heads in transformers, and a simple intervention strategy (SAMI) to diminish or amplify these concepts by scaling the heads' outputs with a single scalar parameter.
papers.conclusion: The proposed pipeline enables concept-agnostic attention head attribution and effective intervention for arbitrary concepts in transformers, offering new insights into the role of attention in concept encoding and control.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge for a wide variety of concepts is sparsely encoded in only 3-10 attention heads across transformer models.
The locations of concept-associated attention modules remain stable before and after LLM post-training, supporting the superficial alignment hypothesis.
The 'French' module is located in later layers, confirming prior work that multilingual LLMs 'think' in English and translate later.
Diminishing the safety module via SAMI increases jailbreaking success on HarmBench by up to +72.7%.
Amplifying the reasoning module improves performance on GSM8K by +1.6%, and suppressing a recognition module in a ViT reduces target label accuracy to 0%.
papers.limitation:
The method does not establish causality for the identified modules, which could be overcomplete or incomplete.
No theoretical sample complexity or stability analysis is provided.
papers.abstract: Transformers have achieved state-of-the-art performance across language and vision tasks. This success drives the imperative to interpret their internal mechanisms with the dual goals of enhancing performance and improving behavioral control. Attribution methods help advance interpretability by assigning model outputs associated with a target concept to specific model components. Current attribution research primarily studies multi-layer perceptron neurons and addresses relatively simple concepts such as factual associations (e.g., Paris is located in France). This focus tends to overlook the impact of the attention mechanism and lacks a unified approach for analyzing more complex concepts. To fill these gaps, we introduce Scalable Attention Module Discovery (SAMD), a concept-agnostic method for mapping arbitrary, complex concepts to specific attention heads of general transformer models. We accomplish this by representing each concept as a vector, calculating its cosine similarity with each attention head, and selecting the TopK-scoring heads to construct the concept-associated attention module. We then propose Scalar Attention Module Intervention (SAMI), a simple strategy to diminish or amplify the effects of a concept by adjusting the attention module using only a single scalar parameter. Empirically, we demonstrate SAMD on concepts of varying complexity, and visualize the locations of their corresponding modules. Our results demonstrate that module locations remain stable before and after LLM post-training, and confirm prior work on the mechanics of LLM multilingualism. Through SAMI, we facilitate jailbreaking on HarmBench (+72.7%) by diminishing "safety" and improve performance on the GSM8K benchmark (+1.6%) by amplifying "reasoning". Lastly, we highlight the domain-agnostic nature of our approach by suppressing the image classification accuracy of vision transformers on ImageNet.

papers.title: Understanding Gated Neurons in Transformers from Their Input-Output Functionality
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between what a neuron reads and what it writes?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a parameter-based method to classify gated neurons in transformers by input-output weight similarity, finding that enrichment neurons dominate early-middle layers while depletion neurons are more common in later layers.
papers.conclusion: The input-output perspective complements activation-dependent analyses and approaches that treat input and output separately, providing insights into how neurons manipulate concepts in the residual stream.
papers.key_findings:
Enrichment neurons dominate in early-middle layers across all 12 models studied, whereas later layers tend more towards depletion neurons.
A large proportion of neurons are input manipulators, with conditional enrichment being the most common class, especially in early-middle layers.
Many neurons exhibit double checking, where gate and input weight vectors are approximately orthogonal but intuitively represent the same concept.
The median cosine similarity between input and output weights is positive in early layers and negative in later layers, indicating a smooth transition in functionality.
Neurons rarely have prototypical weight configurations; instead, they often add novel but related information to the residual stream.
papers.limitation:
The method is parameter-based and therefore limited in scope; it is not designed to replace other neuron analysis methods.
Mathematical similarities of weights may not reflect semantic similarity; orthogonal vectors can represent similar concepts, and similar vectors can represent non-identical concepts.
Case studies of individual neurons may be cherry-picked, focusing on interpretable neurons in later layers, so interpretations may not generalize.
The paper provides only possible interpretations of observed phenomena, not definitive explanations.
future_direction: Extend the method to non-gated activation functions.
Study the evolution of input-output functionalities during model training.
Go beyond the analysis of single neurons to understand how neurons work together within and across classes.
papers.abstract: Interpretability researchers have attempted to understand MLP neurons of language models based on both the contexts in which they activate and their output weight vectors. They have paid little attention to a complementary aspect: the interactions between input and output. For example, when neurons detect a direction in the input, they might add much the same direction to the residual stream ("enrichment neurons") or reduce its presence ("depletion neurons"). We address this aspect by examining the cosine similarity between input and output weights of a neuron. We apply our method to 12 models and find that enrichment neurons dominate in early-middle layers whereas later layers tend more towards depletion. To explain this finding, we argue that enrichment neurons are largely responsible for enriching concept representations, one of the first steps of factual recall. Our input-output perspective is a complement to activation-dependent analyses and to approaches that treat input and output separately.

papers.title: Have Attention Heads in BERT Learned Constituency Grammar?
papers.research_question: Do attention heads in BERT and RoBERTa learn constituency grammar, and how does fine-tuning affect this ability?
papers.core_contribution: Attention heads in BERT and RoBERTa partially learn constituency grammar, with higher layers in BERT and middle layers in RoBERTa showing better ability, and fine-tuning with sentence meaning similarity tasks decreases this ability while natural language inference tasks increase it.
papers.conclusion: Attention heads in BERT and RoBERTa show some constituency grammar ability with layer-specific patterns, fine-tuning affects it differently, and the importance of CGI ability varies between models.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in higher layers of BERT and middle layers of RoBERTa have better constituency grammar inducing (CGI) ability.
Some heads act as a proxy for specific constituency grammar types, but no head fully learns constituency grammar.
Fine-tuning with sentence meaning similarity (SMS) tasks decreases the average CGI ability in upper layers, while natural language inference (NLI) tasks increase it.
For BERT, attention heads with better CGI ability are more important for natural language understanding on QQP and MNLI tasks, but for RoBERTa, this relation is weaker, especially on QQP.
papers.limitation: Attention heads do not fully learn constituency grammar, and it is unclear where syntax information is encoded in BERT.
future_direction: Further study the relations between downstream tasks and the CGI ability in attention heads and explain why different tasks have different effects.
papers.abstract: With the success of pre-trained language models in recent years, more and more researchers focus on opening the "black box" of these models. Following this interest, we carry out a qualitative and quantitative analysis of constituency grammar in attention heads of BERT and RoBERTa. We employ the syntactic distance method to extract implicit constituency grammar from the attention weights of each head. Our results show that there exist heads that can induce some grammar types much better than baselines, suggesting that some heads act as a proxy for constituency grammar. We also analyze how attention heads' constituency grammar inducing (CGI) ability changes after fine-tuning with two kinds of tasks, including sentence meaning similarity (SMS) tasks and natural language inference (NLI) tasks. Our results suggest that SMS tasks decrease the average CGI ability of upper layers, while NLI tasks increase it. Lastly, we investigate the connections between CGI ability and natural language understanding ability on QQP and MNLI tasks.

papers.title: The Kinetics of Reasoning: How Chain-of-Thought Shapes Learning in Transformers?
papers.research_question: How does chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision affect the learning dynamics and generalization of transformers on formal reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: CoT supervision accelerates generalization in transformers on certain reasoning tasks and can be modeled by a kinetic framework, but it also reveals a transient phase of unfaithfulness where answers are correct but reasoning traces are not.
papers.conclusion: CoT supervision advances the take-off point and often raises the ceiling of generalization, but it also reveals a transient faithfulness gap. Mechanistic analyses show that CoT shifts computation from late, serial pipelines toward earlier, more distributed representations.
papers.key_findings:
CoT generally improves task performance but its benefits depend on task complexity.
CoT accelerates generalization but does not overcome tasks with higher algorithmic complexity, such as finding list intersections.
There is a transient trace unfaithfulness phase where models produce correct answers while skipping or contradicting CoT steps.
CoT alters internal transformer computation mechanistically, shifting computation from late, serial pipelines toward earlier, more distributed representations.
Learning curves for both CoT and non-CoT training can be described by a predictable logistic function in log training steps.
papers.limitation:
The synthetic reasoning tasks used are different from real-world reasoning tasks, and the setup does not assess how natural language understanding (i.e., large-scale pretraining) affects CoT reasoning.
The study uses a fixed-size transformer architecture; extending the study to different model sizes could provide more insights on whether model scale affects the learning dynamics.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision can substantially improve transformer performance, yet the mechanisms by which models learn to follow and benefit from CoT remain poorly understood. We investigate these learning dynamics through the lens of grokking by pretraining transformers on symbolic reasoning tasks with tunable algorithmic complexity and controllable data composition to study their generalization. Models were trained under two settings: (i) producing only final answers, and (ii) emitting explicit CoT traces before answering. Our results show that while CoT generally improves task performance, its benefits depend on task complexity. To quantify these effects, we model the accuracy of the logarithmic training steps with a three-parameter logistic curve, revealing how the learning speed and shape vary with task complexity, data distribution, and the presence of CoT supervision. We also uncover a transient trace unfaithfulness phase: early in training, models often produce correct answers while skipping or contradicting CoT steps, before later aligning their reasoning traces with answers. Empirically, we (1) demonstrate that CoT accelerates generalization but does not overcome tasks with higher algorithmic complexity, such as finding list intersections; (2) introduce a kinetic modeling framework for understanding transformer learning; (3) characterize trace faithfulness as a dynamic property that emerges over training; and (4) show CoT alters internal transformer computation mechanistically.

papers.title: Structure Development in List-Sorting Transformers
papers.research_question: How do neural networks develop organized internal structures as they learn? The paper answers this for a single-layer attention-only transformer model trained on sorting lists of numbers.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows how a one-layer attention-only transformer develops organized internal structures (vocabulary-splitting and copy-suppression) while learning to sort lists, and identifies training data characteristics (distribution of gaps between sorted list elements) as a key driver of these specializations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how developmental interpretability can reveal the emergence of structured solutions in transformers, with training data characteristics playing a crucial role in determining the type of specialization that develops.
papers.key_findings:
